callout.label: AP Thinking, Contextualization
callout.body: Understanding what industrialization changed about social order requires knowing what social order looked like BEFORE. The key change: from a society where status was inherited to a society where status was increasingly tied to economic position, but where economic position was determined by ownership of capital (bourgeoisie) or by the sale of labor (proletariat), not by birth. Effective contextualization identifies this shift from hereditary to economic hierarchy as the foundation of 19th-century class conflict.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The New Social Classes: Bourgeoisie and Proletariat

paragraphs.text: The bourgeoisie (industrial middle class, from French "town-dweller"): factory owners, merchants, bankers, lawyers, doctors, engineers, people who earned their social position through accumulated capital and market success, not inherited land. By mid-19th century, the bourgeoisie was economically dominant in industrial societies, though political power (especially in Britain) still rested partly with the landed aristocracy. The bourgeoisie had its own internal stratifications: the great industrialists (iron masters, cotton manufacturers) at the top; the smaller shopkeepers and craftsmen at the bottom.

The industrial proletariat (from Latin "proletarii", those who contribute only their children to the state): factory workers, mine workers, urban day laborers, people who owned nothing but their labor power and had to sell it for wages. The proletariat was created by enclosure (which drove peasants off common land), by the destruction of artisan crafts (by factory competition), and by immigration to industrial cities. By mid-century, the urban proletariat was the largest class in industrialized countries.

Class consciousness and conflict: Marx argued that the proletariat's shared conditions of exploitation would eventually produce class consciousness, the recognition that workers share common interests against the owning class. Whether or not Marx was right about the inevitability of revolution, class conflict was real: strikes, union organizing, political reform movements, and revolutionary uprisings (Paris Commune, 1871) defined 19th-century industrial politics.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Causation
callout.body: Explaining WHY industrialization created these two classes requires tracing specific mechanisms. The bourgeoisie emerged because industrial capital (factories, machines) could generate wealth without land, anyone who could invest in machines could become wealthy. The proletariat emerged because enclosure, artisan displacement, and urban migration created a large population with no property and no choice but to sell labor for wages. Both classes were PRODUCTS of industrialization, not pre-existing groups.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Competing Ideologies: Liberalism, Conservatism, Socialism, and Marxism

paragraphs.text: Liberalism (Adam Smith, John Stuart Mill): freedom of the individual from government interference; free market economics; representative government based on property rights; individual civil liberties. Liberals believed that the market, left to itself, would produce wealth and freedom. They were generally opposed to government regulation of industry. Late 19th-century "New Liberals" accepted some social reform (public education, public health) as compatible with individual liberty.

Conservatism (Edmund Burke, Metternich): respect for tradition, established institutions (monarchy, Church, aristocracy), and gradual rather than radical change. Conservatives were alarmed by the French Revolution and skeptical of Enlightenment rationalism. In the industrial age, some conservatives (like Disraeli's "Tory Democracy" in Britain) accepted reform as a way to prevent revolution, giving the working class enough improvement to keep them loyal to the existing order.

Utopian Socialism (Robert Owen, Charles Fourier, Saint-Simon): early socialists believed that industrial society should be reorganized on cooperative rather than competitive principles. Robert Owen built model factory communities (New Lanark, Scotland) with decent housing, schools, and regulated working hours; he believed that improving workers' conditions would increase productivity and that a model community could transform society through example. Utopian socialists rejected private ownership of production but believed in peaceful, gradual transformation.

Marxism (Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels): Marx's Communist Manifesto (1848) and Das Kapital (1867) provided the most systematic critique of industrial capitalism. Key claims: history is driven by class conflict (historical materialism); the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat by extracting surplus value from their labor; capitalism contains inherent contradictions that will produce economic crises; the proletariat will eventually become class-conscious and overthrow the bourgeoisie through revolution; a communist society without classes or private property will follow. By 1900, Marxist political parties (Social Democrats) were major forces in German, French, and Russian politics.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Comparison
callout.body: Comparing liberalism and socialism as responses to industrialization reveals different diagnoses of the same problem. Liberals diagnosed the problem as TOO MUCH government interference (restrictions on trade, monopolies, aristocratic privilege), their prescription was less government and more market. Socialists diagnosed the problem as the WRONG KIND of property relations (private ownership of production), their prescription was collective ownership of the means of production. Both were responding to the same industrial conditions; they disagreed about the cause of inequality and therefore about the remedy.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Government Response and the Women's Question

paragraphs.text: Political reform : British Reform Acts of 1832, 1867, and 1884 progressively expanded voting rights (from 400,000 voters to ~5 million between 1832 and 1884). Chartism (1838–1857) demanded universal male suffrage, secret ballot, annual parliaments, and payment for MPs, all eventually enacted. By 1900, universal male suffrage existed in Germany (1871), France (1875), and the United States (formally, with severe suppression of Black voters in the South). The pressure for political reform came primarily from working-class and middle-class movements, not from voluntary elite generosity.

Labor legislation : Factory Acts (1833, 1844, 1847) restricted child labor, limited women's and children's hours, and established factory inspectors. Public Health Acts (1848, 1875) created sanitation standards for industrial cities. The Ten Hours Act (1847) limited the working day for women and children to 10 hours, which effectively limited men's hours too since factories couldn't run with only half the workforce.

Bismarckian social insurance : Germany under Bismarck introduced the world's first modern social insurance system: health insurance (1883), accident insurance (1884), old-age and disability insurance (1889). Motivation was explicitly conservative, Bismarck wanted to reduce support for socialist parties by making the state the source of social welfare rather than socialist unions. This model became the template for the 20th-century welfare state.

Women and industrialization : Women and children entered factory work in large numbers, initially because they accepted lower wages. Women's factory work had contradictory effects: it gave women economic independence (their own wages) while subjecting them to exploitation and dangerous conditions. Separate spheres ideology (the belief that women's proper role was domestic) coexisted uncomfortably with the reality of working-class women laboring in factories. The women's suffrage movement (beginning at Seneca Falls, 1848, in the US; building momentum in Britain through the 1860s–1900s) drew on the contradiction between universal rights claims and women's political exclusion, the same contradiction Mary Wollstonecraft had identified in 1792.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Argumentation
callout.body: Did governments respond adequately to the social problems of industrialization in the 19th century? A strong argument requires defining "adequate", adequate by whose standard, and compared to what alternative? Defenders of government response can point to real achievements: child labor restricted, hours limited, public health improved, voting rights expanded. Critics can point to the slow pace, the inadequacy of early reforms, and the suffering that could have been prevented. A nuanced argument acknowledges both and explains which outweighs the other.

extraction.takeaway: Industrialization created two new defining classes: the bourgeoisie (factory owners, merchants, professionals, those who owned capital) and the proletariat (factory workers, miners, urban laborers, those who owned only their labor). Four competing ideologies emerged to explain and address this transformation: liberalism (free market, individual rights, less government) diagnosed the problem as too much restriction; conservatism (tradition, order, gradual change) warned against rapid transformation; utopian socialism (Robert Owen) proposed cooperative communities as alternatives; and Marxism ( Communist Manifesto , 1848) argued that class conflict would inevitably produce revolution and a classless society. Governments responded slowly but eventually: the British Reform Acts expanded voting rights; Factory Acts restricted child labor and limited hours; Bismarck's Germany created the first social insurance system. Women entered industrial work in large numbers, complicating "separate spheres" ideology and fueling the women's suffrage movement. By 1900, the social question, who benefits from industrial wealth?, remained the central political question of the century.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 5.7, Economic Developments and Innovations | AP World History

band.eyebrow: AP World History · Unit 5: Revolutions · Topic 5.7
band.title: The Free Market
band.deck: How industrial capitalism invented new financial institutions, promoted global free trade, and extended economic power far beyond the reach of armies

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Think about how trade worked before industrialization, local markets, guild regulations, mercantilism. Then consider: what new institutions would be needed to finance factories, railroads, and global trade on industrial scale?

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: Understand how corporations, investment banking, and the gold standard created industrial capitalism's financial infrastructure, and how free trade ideology served British industrial interests while blocking development elsewhere.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: Before the Market Revolution

paragraphs.text: Before industrialization, European economies operated under mercantilism , the theory that national wealth came from accumulating gold and silver through trade surpluses, maintained by tariffs, monopolies, and colonial resource extraction. The Dutch East India Company (VOC) and British East India Company had pioneered joint-stock financing in the 17th century, but industrial capitalism required a far more elaborate financial system. Factories, railroads, and global trade networks required capital investment at scales individuals could not provide alone. A Manchester factory owner could not personally fund a railroad; a single investor could not finance a transcontinental line.

Industrial capitalism required new institutions that could pool capital from many investors, limit individual risk, and create markets for buying and selling shares of ownership. The financial revolution that accompanied industrialization was as transformative as the technological revolution, and arguably as important for understanding how the industrial world was organized.

callout.body: Contextualization: Explain how the mercantilist system of the 17th and 18th centuries shaped the economic conditions that industrial capitalism emerged from, and what mercantilism's limits were as an economic framework for industrial-scale production.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Corporations, Banks, and Stock Markets

paragraphs.text: The joint-stock company , in which investors pool capital and share both profits and risks proportionally, was not new in the 19th century, but the limited liability corporation was. Before limited liability, investors in a failed company could be held personally liable for all company debts, potentially losing everything they owned beyond their investment. The UK Companies Act of 1862 established general limited liability, investors could only lose what they had invested, not their entire personal wealth. This single legal change transformed the scale of investment: millions of small investors could now safely participate in large enterprises because their maximum loss was defined.

The stock exchange , a market for buying and selling shares of corporations, made investment liquid. The London Stock Exchange (formalized 1801) and New York Stock Exchange (1817) allowed investors to sell their shares whenever they wanted, rather than being locked into an investment until the company wound down. Investment banks (the House of Morgan, Deutsche Bank, Crédit Lyonnais, the Rothschild family's banking network) specialized in financing large industrial enterprises, floating bonds for railroad construction, and organizing mergers. By 1900, a handful of investment banks controlled the financing of American railroads, German industry, and British overseas investment, and the bankers who ran them were arguably more powerful than most governments.

callout.body: Causation: Explain how limited liability changed the economics of industrial investment. What specific mechanism did it create, and how did it enable industrial enterprises that would have been impossible under the old unlimited liability system?

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Free Trade, the Corn Laws, and Global Integration

paragraphs.text: The most important economic idea of the 19th century was free trade , the argument that removing tariffs and trade barriers would allow each country to specialize in what it produced most efficiently ( comparative advantage ), increasing total wealth for all participants. The architect of this argument was David Ricardo (1817); its most effective political champion was Richard Cobden , who led the campaign to repeal Britain's Corn Laws (1846). The Corn Laws had imposed tariffs on imported grain to protect British landowners; their repeal opened the British market to cheap foreign grain.

But free trade served British interests specifically: Britain was the most industrially advanced nation, producing manufactured goods cheaper than any competitor. Free trade meant British manufactured goods could penetrate every market, while competitors could not yet protect their infant industries from British competition (hence Germany and the United States used protective tariffs while industrializing).

The gold standard , linking currencies to a fixed weight of gold, integrated global financial markets. Britain adopted the gold standard in 1821; most major economies joined by the 1870s–1890s. The gold standard made exchange rates stable and predictable, reducing the risk of international trade and investment. It also constrained government economic policy: governments could not print money to stimulate the economy without gold to back it, which meant deflationary pressure during economic downturns fell on workers (through wage cuts) rather than on creditors (through inflation). The gold standard was an international system that primarily served the interests of creditors and investors.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Economic Power Without Armies: Imperialism Through Finance

paragraphs.text: Economic imperialism extended industrial power without direct colonial rule, through loans, investment, and trade relationships that created dependency without formal annexation. Latin American governments, newly independent from Spain and Portugal but desperate for capital to build infrastructure, borrowed heavily from British banks in the 1820s–1830s. When they defaulted (as many did), British creditors demanded customs revenue as collateral, giving British financial institutions direct control over government finances. By 1900, British investment in Latin America totaled £1 billion; British banks controlled Argentina's railroad system, Chilean copper mining, and Brazilian coffee exports.

The Ottoman Empire borrowed from European banks to modernize its military and infrastructure; by the 1870s, debt service consumed most of Ottoman government revenues, and the Ottoman Public Debt Administration (1881), run by European creditors, directly administered Ottoman tax collection to ensure debt repayment. China's treaty port system , imposed after the Opium Wars, gave foreign merchants extraterritorial rights and control over treaty port trade.

These economic relationships, not formal colonialism, structured much of the world economy by 1900. Economic imperialism was more efficient than direct colonial administration: it extracted profits without the costs of administration and military occupation.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 5.8, Reactions to the Industrial Economy | AP World History

band.eyebrow: AP World History · Unit 5: Revolutions · Topic 5.8
band.title: The Rising
band.deck: How workers organized unions and strikes, abolitionists challenged slavery's connection to industrial capitalism, and reformers transformed education, public health, and social life in the industrial age

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Think about what options workers had when they disagreed with their employer's wages or conditions. Could they quit? Organize? Strike? Vote? Consider: what forms of collective action are available to people who have little individual power?

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: Understand how the labor movement built collective power through unions and strikes; how abolitionism connected to industrial capitalism's cotton economy; and how reform movements transformed education, public health, and prison systems as responses to industrialization's social dislocations.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: The World Before Workers Could Organize

paragraphs.text: In the early decades of industrialization, workers had almost no legal mechanisms to improve their conditions collectively. Trade unions were illegal in Britain under the Combination Acts (1799, 1800), which prohibited workers from organizing to demand higher wages or shorter hours. In the United States, courts routinely ruled that union organizing was a criminal conspiracy in restraint of trade. The legal framework treated the employment relationship as a voluntary contract between free individuals, which meant any collective action by workers to change the terms of that contract was interference with free market principles.

Factory owners could fire organizers, blacklist workers who had joined unions, and call in police or military when workers struck. The political system offered little alternative: in Britain, working-class men did not have the vote until the Reform Acts of 1867 and 1884; in the United States, while working-class white men had formal voting rights, political machines and corporate interests dominated both parties.

Working-class people in the industrial era thus faced a fundamental question: if individual bargaining gave them no power, and the political system offered little, how could they change their conditions?

callout.label: AP Thinking, Contextualization
callout.body: Contextualization: Explain the legal and political context that workers faced in the early industrial period. How did the existing legal framework, treating unions as criminal conspiracies and employment as a free contract , shape what forms of resistance were possible?

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Trade Unions, Strikes, and Collective Power

paragraphs.text: The labor movement built collective power where individuals had none. The Combination Acts in Britain were repealed in 1824, legalizing trade unions for the first time, though unions remained legally restricted and employers found other ways to suppress them. Craft unions organized skilled workers by trade (carpenters, printers, ironworkers); industrial unions organized all workers in an industry regardless of skill. The American Federation of Labor (AFL, 1886), led by Samuel Gompers , focused on "pure and simple unionism", collective bargaining for wages, hours, and conditions, without revolutionary politics.

The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 was the first major labor uprising in the United States: railroad workers walked off the job in response to wage cuts, paralyzing rail traffic in multiple states. State militias and federal troops were called in; dozens of workers were killed. The strike was broken but demonstrated both the potential power of organized workers and the government's willingness to use military force against them.

The Haymarket affair (Chicago, 1886) began as a strike for the eight-hour workday; after police opened fire on strikers, someone threw a bomb, killing several officers. Eight anarchist leaders were tried and convicted in a proceeding widely seen as unjust, four were hanged. Haymarket traumatized the American labor movement and was used to associate unionism with radicalism for decades.

The Pullman Strike (1894), in which railroad workers nationwide refused to handle Pullman Palace Car Company cars in solidarity with striking Pullman workers, was broken when President Cleveland sent federal troops over the objection of the Illinois governor. The strike's leader, Eugene Debs , was imprisoned; after his release he became a socialist. By 1900, the labor movement had achieved some gains, shorter hours in some industries, safety regulations, the legal right to organize in most jurisdictions, but remained politically marginalized in the United States while labor and socialist parties were gaining power in Britain and Europe.

What specific experience, the strike itself, its suppression, or his imprisonment, caused this ideological shift? What does this causal chain reveal about the relationship between labor repression and the growth of radical politics?

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Slavery, Cotton, and the Industrial Economy

paragraphs.text: Abolitionism, the movement to end slavery, was one of the most important reform movements of the industrial era, and it had a direct and complicated relationship with industrial capitalism. The cotton gin (Eli Whitney, 1793) made short-staple cotton profitable, which massively expanded American cotton cultivation, and with it, demand for enslaved labor . By 1850, cotton was the United States' largest export, providing two-thirds of American export earnings. The textile mills of Lancashire and Lowell ran on American cotton, which meant they ran, indirectly, on enslaved labor. The relationship between British and American industrial capitalism and American slavery was not incidental: it was structural.

British abolitionists in the early 19th century argued against slavery partly on moral grounds (the Evangelical Christian tradition) and partly on free-labor economic grounds (that free labor was more productive than enslaved labor). The British Empire abolished slavery in 1833 (effective 1838), largely due to abolitionist organizing, the 1831–32 Baptist War rebellion in Jamaica that demonstrated enslaved people's resistance, and a £20 million payment to slaveholders as compensation.

In the United States, the abolitionist movement intensified through the 1840s–1850s, led by figures including Frederick Douglass (formerly enslaved, the movement's most powerful public voice), William Lloyd Garrison (publisher of The Liberator), and Sojourner Truth. The American Civil War (1861–1865), which ended with the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery, was, among other things, a conflict between two economic systems: industrial wage labor in the North and slave-based plantation agriculture in the South. The Cotton Famine (1861–1865), when the Civil War cut off American cotton to British mills, forced the Lancashire textile industry to seek cotton from Egypt and India, restructuring global cotton supply chains in ways that shaped those economies for generations.

callout.body: Comparison: Compare the British and American abolitionist movements. Both argued against slavery, but they operated in different contexts (a slaveholding empire vs. a slaveholding republic), used different tactics, and achieved abolition through different means. What does comparing these two movements reveal about the relationship between abolitionism and political power?

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Education, Public Health, and the Reform Impulse

paragraphs.text: Industrialization generated a broad reform impulse that extended beyond labor and abolitionism. Public education reform produced mandatory schooling laws: Britain's Education Act 1870 (the Forster Act ) established a system of public elementary schools for children who were not served by existing church schools; subsequent legislation made attendance compulsory and free. In the United States, mandatory schooling laws spread through the states between 1852 (Massachusetts) and 1918, when the last state (Mississippi) required school attendance. The argument for mandatory education combined humanitarian concern (children working in factories rather than learning) with industrial-era economic logic: an industrial economy needed workers who could read instructions, do arithmetic, and follow written rules.

Edwin Chadwick 's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842) documented the direct connection between poverty, poor sanitation, and disease. The germ theory of disease (Pasteur and Koch, 1860s–1870s) provided scientific foundation for sanitation reform. London's Great Stink 1858 , when the Thames, used as an open sewer, became so foul that Parliament was nearly unable to function, directly produced investment in Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system. Public sewer systems, clean water supplies, and building codes spread through industrial cities through the latter half of the 19th century, dramatically reducing death rates from cholera, typhoid, and other waterborne diseases.

Temperance , the movement to limit or prohibit alcohol consumption, was one of the largest mass movements of the industrial era, especially in the United States. Temperance advocates argued that alcohol destroyed working-class family life and economic stability; the WCTU (Women's Christian Temperance Union, founded 1874) was the largest women's organization in 19th-century America. The temperance movement reflected the moral reform impulse of the era: industrialization had created social dislocations that seemed to require moral as well as structural responses.

header.name: Topic 5.9 · Society and the Industrial Age
header.subtitle: Read the narrative, answer three questions across three AP skills, then build your Google Form response and your AI Coach prompt.

band.title: A New Kind of Society: Class, Home, and the Industrial City
band.deck: Industrialization didn’t just change what people made, it remade who they were. New classes, new family roles, and cities that couldn’t keep up.

support.heading: What to do
support.body: Read all three sections, then answer the three questions below. Build your response and submit it to the Google Form, then open your AI Coach.

support.heading: Why it matters
support.body: Topic 5.9 is a causation topic: industrialization caused change in social hierarchies and standards of living. Track who gained, who lost, and why.

sections.label: Historical Development
sections.heading: The Old Order Gets Scrambled

paragraphs.text: Picture walking through Manchester , England, around 1850. Smoke from hundreds of factory chimneys hangs over the rooftops. A few streets away, a well-dressed family steps out of a brick townhouse with a garden. In the same city, two completely different lives are being lived, and both of them are brand new.

For most of history, society was sorted mainly by land and birth: aristocrats on top, peasants and artisans below, with status largely fixed at birth. Industrialization cracked that order open. As factories, railroads, and global trade reorganized how wealth was made, two new social classes rose to define the age.

The first was the middle class , factory owners, merchants, bankers, engineers, and professionals such as lawyers, doctors, managers, and clerks. Their status came from business, skill, and salaries, not noble titles or inherited land, and as industry expanded they grew in numbers and political influence. The second was the industrial working class , the men, women, and children who ran the machines. They sold their labor for wages and worked long shifts in hot, dangerous factories and mines. The widening gap between the owner who collected the profits and the worker who breathed the cotton dust became one of the defining tensions of the 1800s.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Developments and Processes
callout.body: Identify and describe the two new social classes industrialization produced. What made each one *new* compared to the older order of land and birth?

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Two Very Different Homes

paragraphs.text: Industrialization didn’t just change where people worked, it rewired family life, and it did so differently depending on class.

In a working-class family, one paycheck was rarely enough, so wives and children worked too, spinning thread in textile mills, tending machines, or working in mines. Their wages were essential to the family’s survival, and women were routinely paid less than men for the same labor.

In a middle-class family, the pattern flipped. Because one salary could support the household, the wife was increasingly expected not to earn money at all but to manage the home and raise the children. A powerful idea called separate spheres took hold: men belonged to the public world of work and politics, women to the private world of the household. What looked like comfort also meant shrinking opportunity, middle-class women were steered away from education and paid professions toward domesticity . The same revolution pushed working-class women into the workforce and middle-class women out of it.

callout.body: The same force, industrialization, pushed working-class women into wage labor but pushed middle-class women out of it. What economic difference between the two kinds of family caused that divergence?

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The City Couldn’t Keep Up

paragraphs.text: All of this happened inside cities exploding in size faster than anyone could manage. People streamed in from the countryside chasing factory jobs, and the cities simply weren’t built to hold them.

The result was a cluster of challenges: coal smoke filled the air with pollution ; wages that barely covered rent locked families in poverty ; overcrowded districts saw rising crime . With no sewers or clean water, diseases like cholera and typhoid swept through packed neighborhoods, the public health crises of the age. Families crammed into tenements because of severe housing shortages, and cities lacked the infrastructure , clean water, sanitation, transit, to absorb millions of new residents.

Over time these conditions sparked reform, sanitation laws, public health measures, and housing rules (the story of Topic 5.8). For 5.9, the key is to see the whole transformation: industrialization produced a new class structure, new family roles, and new urban problems, reshaping social hierarchies and standards of living from top to bottom.

header.name: Topic 6.1 · Rationales for Imperialism
header.subtitle: Read the narrative, answer three questions across three AP skills, then build your Google Form response and your AI Coach prompt.

band.title: The Language of Conquest
band.deck: Imperialism didn't just happen, it was sold. The 19th century gave industrial powers four ideologies that made conquest feel like science, patriotism, duty, and salvation.

support.heading: What to do
support.body: Read all four sections, then answer the three questions below. Build your response and submit it to the Google Form, then open your AI Coach to pressure-test your thinking.

support.heading: Why it matters
support.body: The Learning Objective asks you to explain how ideologies contributed to the development of imperialism from 1750 to 1900. To do that, you have to understand the four rationales, and how they reinforced one another.

sections.label: Setting the Stage
sections.heading: The World Begins to Shrink

paragraphs.text: By the mid-1800s, something unprecedented was happening to the map. Steam-powered ships now crossed oceans in weeks instead of months. Telegraph cables made communication nearly instantaneous. Factories in Britain, France, and Belgium were churning out textiles, iron rails, and manufactured goods faster than domestic markets could absorb them.

Industrial powers needed two things the rest of the world had in abundance: raw materials to feed their factories, and markets to sell what those factories produced. The logic of expansion became hard to resist. But raw military and economic power alone rarely satisfies a nation for long. People, ordinary citizens, newspaper editors, politicians, clergy, want a story. They want to believe that what their country is doing is not just profitable, but right.
The 19th century gave them four stories. Together, those stories became the ideological architecture of modern imperialism .

callout.label: AP Thinking, Developments and Processes
callout.body: Economic and technological change created the opportunity for empire. As you read, watch how each ideology turns that opportunity into something that feels justified, even noble.

sections.label: Rationale One
sections.heading: Survival of the Fittest (Applied to Nations)

paragraphs.text: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859. Within a decade, European thinkers had stripped his biological framework of its scientific grounding and applied it to human societies. The result was Social Darwinism , the argument that " survival of the fittest " applied not just to species, but to races and civilizations.

The claim was brutal in its simplicity: some peoples were more advanced than others, and this hierarchy was natural and inevitable. European dominance, in this framework, was not a choice or a crime, it was evidence. The fact that European powers could conquer vast territories in Africa and Asia seemed, to Social Darwinists, to prove their superiority. Weakness was its own condemnation.

This ideology was extraordinarily useful because it made conquest feel like natural law rather than political decision. It also created a moral cover for violence: if certain populations were inherently less developed, then dominating them was simply the world working as it was designed to work.

callout.body: Social Darwinism took a scientific idea and bent it to political ends. Be ready to explain exactly what it claimed about race and civilization, and how that claim rationalized control over other peoples.

sections.label: Rationales Two and Three
sections.heading: The Flag and the Mission

paragraphs.text: Nationalism gave imperialism a second engine. As European states consolidated in the 19th century, Germany unifying in 1871, Italy doing the same, national prestige became a political currency. Colonies were a scoreboard. The more territory a nation controlled, the more powerful it appeared to rivals and to its own citizens.

This competition turned imperial expansion into something that felt like patriotism. Citizens who might have questioned the human cost of conquest could be rallied around the flag. Press coverage of military campaigns in Africa or Asia framed them as national achievements. Not acquiring colonies began to feel like national weakness.

Running alongside nationalism was the civilizing mission , the idea that European powers had a duty, not just a right, to transform the societies they controlled. Roads, schools, courts, Christianity: these were offered as gifts from a more advanced civilization to those deemed incapable of governing themselves. The paternalism was thorough. Colonial administrators genuinely believed, in many cases, that they were helping.

What made the civilizing mission particularly effective as an ideology was its moral vocabulary. It transformed extraction into benevolence. The fact that colonized peoples had complex, functioning civilizations of their own, that they were not asking to be transformed, rarely disturbed the logic.

callout.body: Nationalism supplied the competitive drive; the civilizing mission supplied the moral language. Be ready to explain how these two separate ideologies reinforced each other.

sections.label: Rationale Four
sections.heading: The Cross and the Colony

paragraphs.text: Missionary movements gave imperialism its most explicitly moral framing. Protestant and Catholic missionaries poured into Africa, Asia, and the Pacific throughout the 19th century. Their stated goal was salvation: converting indigenous peoples to Christianity.

Missionaries were often genuinely motivated by religious conviction rather than political calculation. Many lived among colonized peoples for decades, learned local languages, and built schools and hospitals. But their presence served imperial purposes whether they intended it to or not. Mission stations often preceded, and sometimes invited, formal colonial control. The disruption of local religious practices weakened existing social structures, making communities more vulnerable to outside authority.

The desire for religious conversion was not cynical in the way Social Darwinism was. But it produced similar effects: it framed colonized peoples as incomplete, in need of what European civilization uniquely possessed. Whether the deficit was racial, cultural, or spiritual, the conclusion was the same, European presence was justified, perhaps required.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 7.1, Shifting Power After 1900 | AP World History: Modern

band.title: When Empires Fall
band.deck: In 1900, the West dominated the global political order, and three enormous land-based empires, the Ottoman, the Russian, and the Qing, still sprawled across Eurasia. By 1923, all three were gone, replaced by new states. In Mexico, a revolution that began with a rigged election rewrote the political and social order itself. None of these collapses had a single cause: in every case, internal weakness and external pressure reinforced each other until the old order broke.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Sort every cause you meet into one of two bins: internal factors (pressures from inside the state, ethnic tension, misrule, peasant land hunger, failed reform) and external factors (pressures from outside, foreign imperialism, military defeat, world war). The AP exam will ask you to explain how the two kinds of factors worked together, not just to list them.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain the internal and external factors behind the Ottoman, Russian, and Qing collapses, trace how political crisis in Russia led to communist revolution in 1917, and explain how the Mexican Revolution challenged the existing political and social order.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: The World in 1900 — Western Dominance, Imperial Strain

paragraphs.text: At the beginning of the 20th century, the West dominated the global political order . Britain ruled a quarter of the world's land and people; France, Germany, and the United States commanded industrial economies, modern navies, and colonial empires. Power in 1900 meant steel production, railroads, battleships, and capital, and the West had nearly all of it.

kt: West dominated the global political order

paragraphs.text: Stretched across Eurasia between these industrial powers lay three older land-based empires : the Ottoman Empire, the Russian Empire, and Qing China. Each was enormous, multiethnic, and ancient, and each was struggling. They had fallen behind in industrialization. Their governments rested on autocratic rulers and weak institutions. Their peasant majorities were poor and land-hungry. Their subject nationalities increasingly wanted out. Europeans called the Ottoman Empire "the sick man of Europe," but the diagnosis fit all three.

The pressures these empires faced came in two kinds. Internal factors grew from inside: ethnic and nationalist tension, misrule, poverty, failed reform. External factors battered them from outside: foreign imperialism, military defeat, and, after 1914, the strain of world war. No single factor brought any of them down. It was always the combination.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Contextualization
callout.body: Topic 7.1 opens Unit 7 with the world as it stood in 1900: Western dominance at its height, and the old land-based empires under strain. Every event in this topic, and most of Unit 7, makes sense only against this backdrop. When you contextualize an essay on 20th-century conflict, start here: a Western-dominated order that the century would systematically dismantle.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The Ottoman and Qing Collapses — Two Empires, One Pattern

paragraphs.text: The Ottoman Empire had ruled for six centuries, but by 1900 nationalist movements in the Balkans had already stripped away much of its European territory, and ethnic tensions ran through what remained. In 1908 a reform movement of young officers and officials, the Young Turks , forced the restoration of constitutional government, trying to save the empire by modernizing it. World War I destroyed it instead: the Ottomans joined the losing side, and defeat in 1918 brought occupation and partition of the empire's Arab lands. Out of the wreckage, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk led a national resistance movement that expelled occupying forces and proclaimed the Republic of Turkey in 1923, a secularizing nation-state where a dynastic empire had stood.

Qing China followed the same pattern with different actors. External pressure came first: a century of unequal treaties, foreign spheres of influence , and military humiliation drained Qing sovereignty. Internal anger answered it, the Boxer Rebellion (1899–1901) rose to expel foreign influence, and its defeat by an eight-nation force brought a crushing indemnity and even deeper foreign control. The dynasty's legitimacy collapsed. In 1911 the Xinhai Revolution spread from a mutiny to a national movement, and in 1912 the boy emperor Puyi abdicated, ending not just the Qing dynasty but two millennia of imperial rule in China, and opening a contested republican era shaped by Sun Yat-sen and his successors.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Comparison
callout.body: The Ottoman and Qing collapses are a ready-made comparison pair. Similarity: both fell to a combination of internal factors (ethnic tension, failed reform, lost legitimacy) and external factors (foreign imperialism, military defeat). Difference: the trigger, the Ottoman Empire was destroyed by defeat in a world war it joined, while the Qing fell to an internal revolution after decades of foreign encroachment. A strong comparison names the shared pattern AND explains what the different triggers reveal.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Russia — From Political Crisis to Communist Revolution

paragraphs.text: Russia's collapse came in stages, and the AP exam cares about the sequence. The first warning was the Revolution of 1905 : humiliating defeat by Japan and the massacre of peaceful petitioners on "Bloody Sunday" set off strikes and mutinies across the empire. Tsar Nicholas II survived by conceding a parliament, the Duma, but kept real power autocratic, leaving every underlying problem unsolved.

World War I broke what 1905 had cracked. Russia's army suffered catastrophic casualties; its cities ran short of food and fuel; its government cycled through ministers while the tsar took personal command at the front and absorbed the blame for every defeat. In the February Revolution of 1917, bread protests and strikes in Petrograd swelled until the soldiers sent to crush them joined them, and Nicholas II abdicated, ending three centuries of Romanov rule.

Power passed to a Provisional Government of liberal politicians, and it failed. It kept Russia in the war the population hated, delayed land reform the peasants demanded, and shared authority uneasily with the workers' and soldiers' councils called soviets . Into that vacuum stepped Lenin and the Bolsheviks with a promise sharp enough to march under: "Peace, Land, and Bread." In the October Revolution , Bolshevik forces seized the levers of power in Petrograd and overthrew the Provisional Government. Political crisis had led, exactly as the CED puts it, to communist revolution .

Notice how external and internal factors alternate and reinforce: the war did not create Russia's weaknesses, it exposed and accelerated them.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Mexico — Revolution Against the Existing Order

paragraphs.text: The challenge to the old order was not confined to Eurasia. In Mexico, Porfirio Díaz had ruled for over three decades, an era of railroads, foreign investment, and growth whose benefits flowed to a narrow elite while most rural Mexicans lost land to great estates. When Díaz rigged yet another election in 1910, the resulting political crisis exploded into the Mexican Revolution (1910–1920), a decade of civil war that drew in every class of Mexican society.

Two leaders show what made the revolution social as well as political. In the south, Emiliano Zapata fought under the banner "Tierra y Libertad", land and liberty, demanding the return of village lands swallowed by haciendas. In the north, Pancho Villa led popular armies of cowboys, miners, and the dispossessed. Their pressure pushed the revolution beyond replacing one president with another and toward remaking society.

The revolution's landmark achievement was the Constitution of 1917 , one of the most radical in the world at the time. It authorized land reform and the breakup of great estates, declared national ownership of subsoil resources (a direct challenge to foreign investors), restricted the power of the Catholic Church, and guaranteed labor rights few industrial democracies matched. This is KC-6.2.II.D in action: a state challenging the existing political and social order , born from political crisis.

kt: the existing political and social order

callout.label: AP Thinking, Argumentation
callout.body: Were these collapses caused more by internal or external factors? A strong claim takes a position and defends it with specifics. For Russia you might argue external (no World War I, no 1917), but 1905 shows the cracks predated the war. For Mexico the case is mostly internal (Díaz's political crisis), with foreign economic influence as a secondary pressure. The best arguments acknowledge the interaction instead of pretending one kind of factor acted alone.

extraction.takeaway: In 1900 the West dominated the global political order , but the old land-based empires were already failing. The Ottoman Empire , strained by ethnic tensions and Young Turk reform, was destroyed by defeat in World War I and replaced by Atatürk's Republic of Turkey (1923). The Qing , hollowed out by foreign imperialism and the failed Boxer Rebellion, fell to the Xinhai Revolution (1911), ending two millennia of imperial rule in China. Russia's political crisis ran from the Revolution of 1905 through the February Revolution, the Provisional Government's failure, and the October Revolution of 1917, when Lenin and the Bolsheviks turned imperial collapse into communist revolution . And in Mexico, the political crisis of Díaz's rigged rule produced the Mexican Revolution and the radical Constitution of 1917 , proof that states around the world were challenging the existing political and social order. In every case the cause was the same combination: internal and external factors , reinforcing each other until the old order broke.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 7.2, Causes of World War I | AP World History: Modern

band.title: The Powder Keg
band.deck: On 28 June 1914, a nineteen-year-old nationalist shot two people in Sarajevo. Five weeks later, every great power in Europe was at war, and within years the fighting reached Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and the world's oceans. The assassination explains almost nothing by itself. What turned a regional crisis into a global war was everything already in place around it: imperialist competition for resources, territorial conflicts in the Balkans, a flawed alliance system, and intense nationalism, the four causes this topic asks you to weigh.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: This is a layered causation topic. Track three layers as you read: the powder (long-term causes, imperial rivalry and nationalism), the fuse (regional conflicts in the Balkans and the alliance system), and the spark (the assassination and the July Crisis). The AP exam will ask you which layer mattered most, so collect evidence for each as you go.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain how imperialist expansion and competition for resources raised tensions among European powers, trace how Balkan conflicts and the flawed alliance system escalated a regional crisis into a global war, and explain how intense nationalism contributed to the outbreak of World War I.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: Europe, 1914 — A Continent Primed to Explode

paragraphs.text: Start with the question this whole topic exists to answer: why did one assassination become a world war? Political murders were not rare in this era, presidents, kings, and an empress had been assassinated in the decades before 1914 without triggering general war. Something about Europe in 1914 turned this one into catastrophe.

kt: why did one assassination become a world war?

paragraphs.text: Part of the answer comes straight from Topic 7.1. The Ottoman Empire you just watched collapse had ruled southeastern Europe for centuries; its long retreat left a power vacuum in the Balkans . New states, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, Greece, scrambled to fill it, while two great powers, Austria-Hungary and Russia, maneuvered behind them. The same imperial decline that ended Topic 7.1 loads the gun in Topic 7.2.

Around that vacuum stood a Europe wound tight by forty years of pressure: empires competing for colonies and resources on every continent, armies and navies swollen by militarism , two rival alliance blocs bound by secret promises, and publics taught by politicians and newspapers that national honor was worth a war. The powder was stacked long before anyone struck the spark.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Contextualization
callout.body: Strong AP writing situates 1914 in the longer story. The Balkan crisis of 1914 only makes sense against the Ottoman collapse (Topic 7.1), the imperial rivalries of Unit 6, and the nationalism unleashed by the revolutions of Unit 5. When you contextualize World War I, reach backward: the war's causes were decades in the making.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Imperialist Expansion and Competition for Resources

paragraphs.text: The first cause the CED names is imperialist expansion and competition for resources . In the Scramble for Africa , European powers seized nearly the entire continent in a generation; at the Berlin Conference (1884–1885) they divided it on paper, without a single African representative in the room. Imperial competition became the normal mode of great-power politics: raw materials , markets , and strategic territory were the scoreboard, and a rival's gain read as your loss.

kt: imperialist expansion and competition for resources

paragraphs.text: That competition repeatedly carried the powers to the edge of war. Germany twice challenged France's position in Morocco, in 1905 and again in 1911, when a German gunboat appeared off Agadir, and both crises ended with Europe's alliance blocs glaring at each other over a colonial dispute. Britain and Germany poured wealth into a naval arms race , building rival fleets of dreadnought battleships. Imperialism taught two dangerous lessons: that great-power status required expansion, and that the next confrontation was always coming.

callout.body: Imperial competition is a long-term cause , powder, not spark. On the exam, connect it to the outbreak of war through a mechanism: colonial crises (Morocco 1905, 1911) hardened the alliance blocs, the naval race militarized Anglo-German rivalry, and decades of competition normalized the idea that great powers settle scores by force.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The Balkans, the Spark, and the Flawed Alliance System

paragraphs.text: Europeans called the Balkans the 'powder keg of Europe' , and the label was earned. As Ottoman power receded, Serb, Bulgarian, and Romanian nationalism rose to claim the space, and the Balkan Wars (1912–1913) redrew the regional map twice in two years. Serbia emerged enlarged and emboldened; Austria-Hungary, a multiethnic empire with millions of South Slav subjects, watched Serbian ambition as an existential threat; Russia stood behind Serbia as patron and protector.

The spark came on 28 June 1914, when Gavrilo Princip , a Bosnian Serb nationalist, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand , heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo. Vienna blamed Serbia, secured Germany's unconditional backing, the famous 'blank check' , issued an ultimatum drafted to be refused, and on 28 July declared war on Serbia . On its own, this was a third Balkan crisis in three years.

The flawed alliance system made sure it did not stay regional. Europe stood divided into the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain), bound by secret commitments and watching each other with mutual suspicion. Russia mobilized to back Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia, then on Russia's ally France; Germany's invasion route ran through neutral Belgium, which brought Britain in. In one week of August 1914, a chain reaction of alliance obligations turned a regional conflict into a global conflict , exactly the escalation the CED describes.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Causation
callout.body: Keep the escalation chain in order, it is the skeleton of any 7.2 essay: assassination (28 June) → ultimatum and blank check (July) → Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia (28 July) → Russian mobilization → German declarations on Russia and France → invasion of Belgium → Britain enters (4 August). Each link is an alliance commitment doing exactly what it promised, that is what made the system 'flawed': it was designed to deter a war and instead guaranteed its spread.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Intense Nationalism — and the Problem of Weighing Causes

paragraphs.text: Running through every other cause was intense nationalism . In the great powers, national pride fueled militarism : Germany demanded its 'place in the sun,' France nursed the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, and mass-circulation newspapers demonized rival nations until compromise looked like cowardice. In the Balkans, nationalism took the form of self-determination movements : Princip killed the Archduke in the name of South Slavs who wanted out of Austria-Hungary. Nationalism was the accelerant, it made imperial rivalry prouder, regional conflict fiercer, and every alliance obligation feel like a matter of national honor.

So which cause mattered most? Historians have argued for a century, and the AP exam invites you into the argument. Was the alliance system the decisive escalator, the machine that turned one murder into general war? Or was the machine only dangerous because nationalism and imperial rivalry had loaded it? Notice the structure of the question: it is the same powder versus spark distinction you practiced in Topic 7.1 with internal and external factors, and it returns in Topic 7.9, the causation capstone of this unit.

callout.body: A strong relative-significance argument does three things: takes a clear position ("the flawed alliance system was the most significant cause"), supports it with specific evidence (the blank check, the mobilization chain of August 1914), and addresses the alternative (the assassination was a spark that the alliance system, not nationalism alone, converted into global war). Ranking causes without defending the ranking is description, not argument.

extraction.takeaway: World War I had four braided causes, and the CED names them all in one sentence. Imperialist expansion and competition for resources , the Scramble for Africa, the Berlin Conference, the Moroccan crises, the naval race, made rivalry the normal state of great-power politics. Territorial and regional conflicts concentrated that rivalry in the Balkans, the powder keg left behind by Ottoman decline, where the Balkan Wars (1912–1913) and the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (28 June 1914) supplied the spark. The flawed alliance system , Triple Alliance vs. Triple Entente, blank check, mobilization chain, escalated Austria-Hungary's war on Serbia into a general European war within a week. And intense nationalism accelerated everything: great-power pride, militarism, demonized rivals, and Balkan self-determination movements. One assassination became a global conflict because all four causes were already in place, your job is to explain how they combined, and to argue which mattered most.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 7.3, Conducting World War I | AP World History: Modern

band.title: The Total War
band.deck: The war that began in August 1914 was supposed to be over by Christmas. Instead, machine guns froze the armies into trenches, and victory came to depend on which society could out-produce and out-endure the other. So governments mobilized everything: factories and food, posters and films, artists and novelists, national myths, and the colonies. World War I became the first total war, and its new technology drove casualties to levels no one had imagined. This topic asks how governments waged that war, and what it cost.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: This topic runs on two Key Concepts, and you need both. Track mobilization (how governments used propaganda, art, media, intensified nationalism, and the colonies, to wage total war) and technology (how machine guns, trenches, tanks, aircraft, and gas drove casualties to unprecedented levels). The strongest answers connect the two: total mobilization fed societies into an industrial battlefield.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain why World War I is considered the first total war, describe how governments mobilized populations in home countries and colonies, and explain how new military technology led to increased levels of wartime casualties.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: From Chain Reaction to Total War

paragraphs.text: Topic 7.2 ended with the alliance chain reaction detonating: in one week of August 1914, a Balkan crisis became a general European war. Every government expected a short one, troops were promised they would be home before Christmas . The machine gun canceled that promise. Massed attacks failed against entrenched firepower, the armies dug in, and the Western Front froze into a line of trenches from the English Channel to Switzerland.

Stalemate changed the question. If no army could win quickly, victory would belong to the society that could produce more shells, feed more soldiers, absorb more losses, and keep believing longer. That is the logic of total war : a war in which civilians, industries, and government institutions are all mobilized for the war effort, not just the armies. World War I was the first total war , and this topic is about what that mobilization looked like.

Governments converted factories to munitions, rationed food and fuel, took control of railroads and prices, brought women into war industries, and, just as deliberately, took control of what their citizens saw, read, and believed. The home front became a front.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Continuity and Change
callout.body: Warfare changed in kind, not just degree. Earlier wars mobilized armies and treasuries; World War I mobilized societies, labor, industry, media, belief, and empire. When the AP asks what made this war 'total,' the answer is the erasure of the line between soldier and civilian: everyone was part of the war effort, which is also why everyone became a target of persuasion.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Propaganda, Art, Media, and Intensified Nationalism

paragraphs.text: The Key Concept lists the strategies precisely: governments used political propaganda, art, media, and intensified forms of nationalism to mobilize their populations. Propaganda came first and loudest, posters, pamphlets, and films that demonized the enemy and made enlistment a personal duty. Lord Kitchener's 'Your Country Needs You' in Britain and 'Uncle Sam Wants You' in the United States aimed a pointing finger at every man of military age.

kt: political propaganda, art, media, and intensified forms of nationalism

paragraphs.text: The state also enlisted culture itself. Governments commissioned official war artists to paint the conflict; newsreels and radio broadcasts carried curated images of the war into theaters and homes, sustaining morale through years of casualty lists. Britain's secret Wellington House propaganda bureau even hired famous novelists to write for the cause. Censorship worked alongside celebration, the same ministries that produced the art controlled what newspapers could print.

Beneath it all ran intensified nationalism . The national pride that helped cause the war (Topic 7.2) was now weaponized to sustain it: the war was framed as a struggle for national honor and survival , wrapped in myths of destiny, Germany's Weltpolitik and its claim to a 'place in the sun,' France's sacred soil, Britain's defense of civilization. A war for survival cannot be compromised on; that framing kept exhausted societies fighting.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Sourcing
callout.body: Propaganda is perfect HIPP practice. A recruitment poster is never a window onto the war, it is a weapon aimed at an audience. Read it for historical situation (Britain needed volunteers before conscription), intended audience (young men and the communities watching them), purpose (turn enlistment into obligation), and point of view (duty and glory, costs invisible). What a propaganda source omits is evidence too.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Mobilizing the Colonies

paragraphs.text: The Key Concept's parenthesis is easy to skip and heavily tested: governments mobilized populations 'both in the home countries and the colonies.' A European war became a world war partly because Europe ruled the world, and it billed its empires for the fight.

kt: 'both in the home countries and the colonies.'

paragraphs.text: Colonial troops served on every front. Over a million Indian soldiers fought for the British Empire, from the Western Front to the Middle East; France deployed hundreds of thousands of West African, North African, and Indochinese troops. Beyond soldiers, colonies supplied labor and resources , porters and laborers by the hundred thousand, plus raw materials, food, and taxes. The fighting itself spread to Africa, the Middle East, and the Pacific as the belligerents attacked each other's colonies.

kt: Africa, the Middle East, and the Pacific

paragraphs.text: File this away for Unit 8: colonial subjects who were told the war defended freedom and self-determination noticed that the freedom was not meant for them. The sacrifice of 1914–1918 became an unpaid invoice that independence movements would present after both world wars.

One sentence on Indian or West African troops, and one on the war's spread to Africa, the Middle East, and the Pacific, turns a partial answer into a complete one.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: New Technology and the Human Cost

paragraphs.text: The second Key Concept is one sentence: new military technology led to increased levels of wartime casualties . The chain starts with the machine gun , which made massed infantry attacks suicidal and drove both sides into trench warfare , a fortified stalemate where offensives bought yards with lives. Tanks were invented to break the deadlock; aircraft evolved from reconnaissance to fighters and bombers in four years; chemical weapons , chlorine and mustard gas , burned lungs and blinded survivors, inflicting damage that lasted lifetimes.

kt: new military technology led to increased levels of wartime casualties

paragraphs.text: Notice the TEC theme working: each innovation answered a battlefield problem (its intended consequence ) and created a new horror (its unintended consequence ). Machine guns were meant to defend; they produced the trench stalemate. The stalemate produced battles of attrition , the Somme and Verdun each consumed hundreds of thousands of men for a few miles of mud.

Now put the two Key Concepts together. Total-war mobilization fed entire societies into a battlefield ruled by industrial technology, and the result was roughly 20 million dead and as many wounded, casualties on a scale no previous war had approached. The scale forced ethical questions that outlived the war: What may a state demand of its citizens? Should any weapon be beyond use? Soldiers like Wilfred Owen answered the propaganda directly, his poem about a gas attack ends by calling 'Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori' 'the old Lie.'

callout.body: A strong 7.3 argument connects the Key Concepts instead of listing them. Claim: World War I's unprecedented casualties came from the combination of total mobilization and industrial technology, machine guns created the stalemate, stalemate made the war long, and total war kept whole societies feeding the front. Evidence: the Somme, conscription, and gas. Then complicate it: propaganda's framing of the war as national survival is why no government stopped paying the cost.

extraction.takeaway: World War I was the first total war : civilians, industries, and government institutions were all mobilized for the war effort. Governments used the strategies the CED names, political propaganda (Kitchener, Uncle Sam), art and media (official war artists, newsreels, censorship), and intensified nationalism (war as national survival, Weltpolitik), to mobilize populations both in the home countries and the colonies : over a million Indian soldiers, hundreds of thousands of African and Indochinese troops, plus colonial labor and resources. Meanwhile new military technology , machine guns and trench warfare, tanks, aircraft, and mustard gas, led to increased levels of wartime casualties : roughly 20 million dead, attrition battles like the Somme and Verdun, and ethical questions about the human cost of war that the 20th century never stopped asking. The formula to remember: mobilization plus industrial technology equals war on an unprecedented scale.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 7.4, Economy in the Interwar Period | AP World History: Modern

band.title: When the Money Stopped
band.deck: Total war left the world's economies exhausted; then, in October 1929, the American stock market crashed and the exhaustion became collapse. Unemployment, business failures, and a global trading system in ruins forced every kind of government to answer the same question: what is the state's job when the economy fails? The era of hands-off government was over. A democracy, a fascist dictatorship, a communist state, and two popular-nationalist governments in Latin America gave four very different answers, and comparing them is exactly what this topic asks of you.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Hold one similarity and many differences. The similarity is the Key Concept itself: after WWI and the Depression, every government took a more active role in economic life . The differences are ideological, track for each response: who controls the economy, who benefits, and what happens to individual rights. The Soviet case gets its own Key Concept; give its human cost special attention.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain why governments intervened after World War I and the onset of the Great Depression, explain how the Soviet Five-Year Plans controlled the economy and what they cost the population, and compare the New Deal, the fascist corporatist economy, and the state-led economies of Brazil and Mexico.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: The Bill Comes Due

paragraphs.text: The total war of Topic 7.3 was an economic event as much as a military one. Four years of feeding whole societies into the front left Europe exhausted , governments buried in debt, currencies inflated, trade networks broken, and recovery propped up by American loans. The world economy of the 1920s was a convalescent leaning on one crutch.

In October 1929 the crutch snapped. The stock market crash in New York triggered the Great Depression : banks failed, credit vanished, and the disaster traveled outward along every artery of the connected world economy. By 1932, unemployment reached a quarter of the workforce in the United States and Germany; business failures spread by the tens of thousands; global trade collapsed to a fraction of its former volume. Coffee rotted in Brazil while bread lines lengthened in Berlin, the market had failed everywhere at once.

The crisis ended an era. Through the 19th century, the reigning answer had been laissez-faire, government keeps its hands off the economy. After 1929 that answer was politically dead. The Key Concept states the turn precisely: following World War I and the onset of the Great Depression, governments began to take a more active role in economic life . The question was no longer whether to intervene. It was how , and the answers split along ideology.

callout.body: Chain the causes in order: total war exhausts the world economy → the 1929 crash turns exhaustion into collapse → unemployment, business failures, and collapsing trade discredit hands-off government → states intervene. On the exam, the Depression is both an effect (of WWI's economic damage) and a cause (of intervention everywhere, and, as Topic 7.6 will show, of the next war).

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Two Answers in the West: The New Deal and the Corporatist Economy

paragraphs.text: The first illustrative example is the New Deal , the democratic answer. Franklin D. Roosevelt's program promised relief, recovery, reform : the Social Security Act built a permanent safety net for the old and unemployed; the Works Progress Administration (WPA) put millions directly on the government payroll, building roads, bridges, schools, even murals and plays. The New Deal did not abolish capitalism or suspend the Constitution; it permanently expanded government's role inside a democracy , with courts, elections, and unions intact.

kt: expanded government's role inside a democracy

paragraphs.text: Mussolini's Italy gave the authoritarian answer: the fascist corporatist economy . The state organized corporations , sector-by-sector bodies partnering government with major industries, to direct production toward nationalist goals. Independent labor unions were curtailed and absorbed into state syndicates; strikes were banned. Fascist economics pursued self-sufficiency and national power, rearmament, prestige projects, autarky, and paid for them with individual rights . Intervention here served the state, not the citizen.

callout.body: Here is your first precise comparison pair. Similarity: both the New Deal and the corporatist economy put the state deep into economic life, public payrolls, industrial policy, social programs. Difference: the New Deal worked within democratic accountability (elections, courts, unions survived); the corporatist economy dismantled exactly those checks. The difference is not degree of intervention, it is what the intervention served.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The Soviet Five-Year Plans — Control and Its Cost

paragraphs.text: The Soviet Union gets its own Key Concept, and the wording deserves close reading: the government controlled the national economy through the Five-Year Plans , often implementing repressive policies , with negative repercussions for the population . Stalin's first Five-Year Plan (1928–1932) , launched even before the Wall Street crash, aimed at rapid industrialization at any cost: steel mills, dams, tractor factories, entire cities like Magnitogorsk willed into existence by state command.

kt: controlled the national economy through the Five-Year Plans

paragraphs.text: The cost fell on the countryside. Forced collectivization seized peasant land and livestock into state farms; peasant resistance , millions slaughtered their animals rather than surrender them, was answered with deportations to forced labor camps. Grain quotas stripped villages bare while the state exported food to buy machinery. In Ukraine the result was the Holodomor : a famine that killed millions in 1932–1933 while the harvests that could have saved them were sold abroad.

Hold both halves of the truth. The Plans worked, by their own measure: the USSR industrialized in a decade at a speed no market economy had matched, which is why the Soviet model looked attractive to many observers during the capitalist Depression. But the Key Concept's verdict is the one to remember: state control prioritized output over human well-being , and the population paid.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Brazil, Mexico, and the Comparison Frame

paragraphs.text: The third illustrative example often gets skipped, do not skip it: governments with strong popular support in Brazil and Mexico . In Brazil, Getúlio Vargas answered the collapse of coffee prices with a state-led national economy: state-owned enterprises in steel and oil, and import substitution industrialization (ISI) , building at home the manufactured goods Brazil had always imported.

kt: governments with strong popular support in Brazil and Mexico

paragraphs.text: Mexico's intervention delivered the unfinished promises of its Revolution, the one you studied in Topic 7.1. Under Lázaro Cárdenas , the government carried out sweeping land reform , distributing tens of millions of acres to villages, finally honoring the demand Zapata had died for. Then in 1938 Cárdenas nationalized the oil industry , expelling foreign companies and founding Pemex , a state oil monopoly that made economic sovereignty a matter of national pride. Crowds filled the Zócalo to donate jewelry and chickens toward the compensation payments: intervention with strong popular support , exactly as the CED says.

Now assemble the comparison frame this topic is built for: four answers to one crisis , democratic (New Deal), fascist (corporatist economy), communist (Five-Year Plans), and popular-nationalist (Brazil and Mexico). The similarity is universal: a more active state. The differences are ideological: who controls, who benefits, what happens to rights. And keep the thread for Topic 7.6, the Depression's despair is fuel for the extremism that causes the next war.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 7.5, Unresolved Tensions After World War I | AP World History: Modern

band.title: The Empire That Would Not End
band.deck: The empires you watched collapse after 1900 left their colonies on the table, and the victors of World War I did not hand them back, they redistributed them. Between the wars, Western and Japanese imperial states predominantly maintained the control they had, gained more through mandates and conquest, and faced a rising tide of anti-imperial resistance. The Learning Objective asks the question directly: what changed in territorial holdings, and what stayed exactly the same?

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Hold two ideas at once: continuity (imperial control was predominantly maintained) and change (territory was gained through mandates and conquest, and resistance was rising). For every development, ask: is this control MAINTAINED, territory GAINED, or empire CHALLENGED? Sort everything into those three buckets and the topic snaps into focus.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain how Western and Japanese imperial states maintained and expanded control between the wars, how the League of Nations mandate system transferred former German and Ottoman territories to Britain and France, and how the Indian National Congress and West African resistance challenged imperial rule.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: A Peace That Settled Nothing

paragraphs.text: In Topic 7.1 you watched empires crack, the Ottoman , German , Austro-Hungarian, and Russian empires all collapsed in the war's aftermath, leaving vast stretches of territory on the table . In Topics 7.2 and 7.3 you saw the total war that brought them down. When the guns finally stopped in 1918, the map of the world was waiting to be redrawn, and the victors held the pen.

Here is the move that catches students off guard: those colonies did not become free. The empires of the losers were absorbed by the winners . Between the two world wars, Western and Japanese imperial states predominantly maintained control over the colonial holdings they already had, and several of them gained more . The Learning Objective frames the whole topic as a question of continuities and changes in territorial holdings : what changed, and what stayed the same?

kt: continuities and changes in territorial holdings

paragraphs.text: The core claim is the one to carry through every section: empires did not end in 1918, they reorganized. The war redrew borders and changed which flag flew where, but the underlying fact of imperial control held. What changed sat on top of a deep continuity; what stayed the same generated tensions that the peace left unresolved.

kt: empires did not end in 1918, they reorganized.
