callout.label: AP Thinking, Continuity & Change
callout.body: Train yourself to sort every development into one of three buckets. MAINTAINED (continuity): Britain and France keep their pre-war empires. GAINED (change): mandates and Japanese conquest add new territory. CHALLENGED (change): the Indian National Congress and West African resistance push back. A continuity-and-change essay is really just naming what persisted, naming what shifted, and explaining how they relate.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The Mandate System: Empire by Another Name

paragraphs.text: The first illustrative example of territorial gain is the League of Nations mandate system . Former German colonies were transferred to Great Britain and France , German East Africa (Tanzania) to Britain, German South West Africa (Namibia) to South African control. On paper this was not conquest; it was international trusteeship, blessed by the new League of Nations.

Listen to the rhetoric: the mandates existed, the Covenant said, to prepare territories for self-governance , to hold them in trust until their peoples were "able to stand by themselves." The reality was continued colonial exploitation . The same resources were extracted, the same populations governed without consent, the same flag of empire flew, only the legal label had changed. The mandate system is the Key Concept's "additional territories through treaty settlement" wearing the costume of humanitarian progress.

The pattern repeated in the former Ottoman lands. The wartime Sykes-Picot Agreement (1916) had already secretly divided the Middle East into British and French spheres; postwar mandates made it official, handing Syria and Lebanon to France and Iraq to Britain. Borders were drawn without regard to ethnic and sectarian boundaries , straight lines serving imperial convenience, sowing future conflict that would outlast the century.

kt: without regard to ethnic and sectarian boundaries

A strong argument names that contradiction explicitly: the rhetoric of "tutelage" and "sacred trust" legitimized empire precisely when colonized peoples were demanding the opposite. Quote the gap, don't just describe the policy.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Japan's Expansion — Gains by Conquest

paragraphs.text: Not every gain came dressed as a mandate. Japan was an imperial state that expanded the old-fashioned way, by conquest . In 1931 its army seized Manchuria, and in 1932 it installed Manchukuo , a puppet state with a borrowed emperor and a flag of its own, but with every real decision made in Tokyo.

Japan wrapped its expansion in anti-imperial language. The Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere was advertised as Asian unity against Western imperialism , Asia for the Asians, free of European masters. In practice it served Japanese interests : a new empire built on the rhetoric of ending empires. The conquest drove rising tensions with China and the Western powers that the fragile interwar order could not contain.

kt: rising tensions with China and the Western powers

paragraphs.text: This is the Key Concept's other route to "additional territories": where mandates were gains by treaty settlement , Manchukuo was a gain by conquest . And it points forward, Japanese expansion in East Asia is one of the lit fuses that foreshadows the next war in Topic 7.6.

kt: foreshadows the next war in Topic 7.6.

callout.body: Compare the two paths to gain. Similarity: both the mandate system and Manchukuo expanded imperial control after WWI. Difference: mandates gained territory by treaty and called it trusteeship; Japan gained territory by conquest and called it liberation. sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The Resistance: India, West Africa, and the Change Beneath

paragraphs.text: Against the continuity of maintained empire ran the change the Key Concept names last: anti-imperial resistance . In India, the Indian National Congress , founded back in 1885 , moved from polite petitions toward mass protest , learning to mobilize an entire subcontinent. Postwar discontent exploded after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) , when British troops fired on an unarmed crowd at Amritsar, killing hundreds. The massacre galvanized the broader independence movement , turning moderate grievance into a mass demand for self-rule.

In French West Africa, resistance took the shape of strikes, protests, and congresses challenging French colonial rule . These were organized political acts, workers and educated elites building institutions to press their claims, and beneath them grew a nationalist sentiment and a demand for self-determination that echoed from Amritsar to Dakar.

Now assemble the synthesis the Learning Objective wants: imperial control was predominantly maintained (continuity) even as mandates and conquest redrew the map (change) and resistance built pressure (change). The tensions this left unresolved, arbitrary borders, conquered peoples, colonized populations demanding freedom, are the fuse for Topic 7.6 , and a thread to carry into the 7.9 causation capstone.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 7.6, Causes of World War II | AP World History: Modern

band.title: Four Roads to One War
band.deck: The unresolved tensions you studied in Topic 7.5 did not stay unresolved, they exploded into a second total war. The College Board names four causes of World War II in a single sentence: a failed peace, a global economic collapse, continued imperialist ambition, and, its own word, "especially" the rise of fascist and totalitarian regimes. This reading walks each road, then asks the question the framework dares you to answer: which cause mattered most?

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: The Key Concept is one long sentence listing four causes. Number them as you read: (1) the unsustainable peace, (2) the Great Depression, (3) continued imperialist aspirations, (4) and especially the rise of fascist and totalitarian regimes . Watch the word "especially", the CED is ranking its own causes, and the topic asks you to evaluate that ranking, not just repeat it.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain how the unsustainable peace after World War I, the Great Depression, and continued imperialist aspirations escalated tensions in the 1930s, and how the rise of fascist and totalitarian regimes, especially Nazi Germany under Hitler, turned those tensions into aggressive militarism and war.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: The Twenty Years' Crisis

paragraphs.text: In Topic 7.5 you left the interwar world full of unresolved tensions , arbitrary mandate borders, conquered peoples under puppet states, colonized populations demanding self-determination, and a Germany nursing the wounds of a peace it never accepted. This topic is what happens when those tensions resolve violently . The two decades between the wars were less a peace than a pause.

The Key Concept compresses the whole story into one sentence, and it pays to read that sentence as a four-part list : World War II was caused by the unsustainable peace settlement after World War I, the global economic crisis engendered by the Great Depression , continued imperialist aspirations , and, note the word, especially the rise to power of fascist and totalitarian regimes that produced the aggressive militarism of Nazi Germany under Adolf Hitler .

kt: global economic crisis engendered by the Great Depression
especially the rise to power of fascist and totalitarian regimes
aggressive militarism of Nazi Germany under Adolf Hitler

paragraphs.text: That little word "especially" is the framework doing your historical thinking out loud. The CED is not just listing causes, it is ranking them, naming the rise of the regimes as the most significant. Your job in this topic is to test that ranking: build the case for it, build the case against it, and decide what you actually think.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Causation
callout.body: Distinguish two kinds of cause as you read. BACKGROUND CONDITIONS (the unsustainable peace, the Depression) created grievance and desperation but did not themselves start a war. The PROXIMATE cause (the rise of fascist regimes and their aggressive militarism) is the actor that converted those conditions into invasions. The CED's "especially" is a claim that the trigger outweighed the conditions, exactly the kind of weighting the 7.9 capstone will ask you to argue.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Two Conditions: A Failed Peace and a Broken Economy

paragraphs.text: Cause one is the unsustainable peace settlement . The Treaty of Versailles (1919) saddled Germany with crushing reparations , stripped away territory , and, through the war-guilt clause, forced it to accept sole blame for the war. The result was a deep well of humiliation, resentment, and economic burden : a widespread German conviction that the peace was a betrayal to be overturned, not a settlement to be honored. That bitterness became fertile ground for radical political movements promising to tear the treaty up.

kt: fertile ground for radical political movements

paragraphs.text: Cause two is the global economic crisis engendered by the Great Depression , the collapse you studied in Topic 7.4, now seen as a cause of war. Mass unemployment and desperation discredited democratic governments that could not fix the crisis, and made the extremists' promises of order, revival, and national renewal suddenly attractive to people with nothing left to lose. The Depression did not start the war by itself, but it weakened the democracies and strengthened the radicals .

kt: global economic crisis engendered by the Great Depression
weakened the democracies and strengthened the radicals

callout.body: Notice how Topics 7.4 and 7.5 fold into 7.6. The Great Depression (7.4) is no longer just an economic episode, here it is a CAUSE of the next war. The unsustainable peace (7.5's "peace that settled nothing") is no longer just an unresolved tension, here it is the first cause on the CED's list. Topic 7.6 reframes earlier content as causation. Use those callbacks as evidence, not just review.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Especially: The Rise of the Regimes

paragraphs.text: Cause three is the one the CED calls especially decisive: the rise to power of fascist and totalitarian regimes . In Germany, Hitler and the Nazi Party capitalized on the nationalist resentment Versailles had bred and on the desire for revenge , promising to restore Germany's glory , rebuild its military , and reclaim lost territories .

kt: rise to power of fascist and totalitarian regimes

paragraphs.text: Those were not just slogans. They became aggressive expansionist policy : rearmament in open defiance of Versailles, the remilitarization of the Rhineland, and the annexation of neighboring lands. This is where the first two causes converge, Versailles supplied the grievance , the Depression supplied the desperation , and the Nazi regime supplied the militarized will to act on both .

kt: militarized will to act on both

paragraphs.text: Cause four, continued imperialist aspirations , shows the same pattern was not Germany's alone. The 1930s saw aggressive militarism across three regions: German expansion in Europe, Italian ambitions under Mussolini in the Mediterranean and Africa, and Japanese expansion in Asia, the Manchukuo of Topic 7.5 the leading edge. Three expansionist powers, one militarized appetite for empire.

callout.body: Take "especially" as a thesis to test. The case FOR: without Hitler's regime, the grievances of Versailles and the pain of the Depression need not have produced a world war, many countries suffered both without invading their neighbors. The case AGAINST: without the failed peace and the Depression, Hitler never rises at all; the conditions made the trigger possible. A strong answer names a criterion for "most significant" and defends a position, it does not simply list four causes and stop.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The Multiplier: A League That Could Not Act

paragraphs.text: The four causes had an enabler that the Key Concept does not list but every account includes: the League of Nations' inability to respond effectively to aggression. When Japan seized Manchuria and Italy invaded Ethiopia, the League issued condemnations but imposed no real consequences , and the expansionist powers were watching.

kt: League of Nations' inability to respond effectively

paragraphs.text: Aggression that went unpunished emboldened the aggressors. Diplomacy curdled into appeasement , most infamously at Munich in 1938, where handing Hitler the Sudetenland only fed his appetite. Each unanswered move taught the same lesson: there was no price to pay for aggression, and the road from appeasement ran straight to 1939 .

Now assemble the answer the Learning Objective wants: World War II had four causes the CED names, a failed peace, a global depression, imperial ambition, and especially the rise of fascist and totalitarian regimes, multiplied by a collective-security system too weak to stop any of them. header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 7.7, Conducting World War II | AP World History: Modern

band.title: Mobilizing Everything
band.deck: World War II was a total war, and every great power mobilized the same things: propaganda, art, media, intensified nationalism, and the full weight of the economy. But the College Board asks a comparative question, not just THAT governments mobilized, but HOW their methods were alike and different. Two democracies, Britain and the United States, persuaded free publics; two totalitarian states, Germany and the USSR, controlled them. And new technology, the atomic bomb, fire-bombing, drove casualties to heights even World War I never reached.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Hold one similarity and one difference. The similarity: all four states mobilized propaganda, art, media, nationalism, and resources for total war. The difference: totalitarian states used ideology to repress basic freedoms and dominate daily life ; democracies did not. For each leader, Churchill, Roosevelt, Hitler, Stalin, ask: what method, and what limit?

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain how governments used propaganda, media, and nationalism to mobilize home and colonial populations, compare democratic and totalitarian mobilization, and explain how the atomic bomb, fire-bombing, and total war drove wartime casualties higher.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: Total War, Round Two

paragraphs.text: You already know the total-war playbook . In Topic 7.3 you saw whole societies mobilized for World War I, propaganda, rationing, economies turned to the front. In Topic 7.6 you saw how the second war began. Now watch the playbook run again, on a larger and deadlier scale.

The Key Concept opens flatly: World War II was a total war. Governments used a variety of strategies, political propaganda, art, media, and intensified forms of nationalism , to mobilize populations both in the home countries and the colonies or former colonies for the purpose of waging war. That parenthetical matters: empires drew troops and resources from across the globe, not just from home.

kt: World War II was a total war.

The CED supplies the comparison set itself, two Western democracies (Britain under Churchill, the U.S. under Roosevelt) and two totalitarian states (Germany under Hitler, the USSR under Stalin). Same war, four mobilizations.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Comparison
callout.body: Build a two-column table in your head. SHARED METHODS go in the middle: propaganda, art, media, intensified nationalism, full resource mobilization, every state used them. The DIFFERENCE goes in the margins: totalitarian states used ideology (fascism, communism) to repress basic freedoms and dominate daily life; democracies mobilized free publics by persuasion. A strong comparison names a precise shared method AND a precise difference, not just "they were similar and different."

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The Democracies: Churchill and Roosevelt

paragraphs.text: Great Britain under Winston Churchill mobilized through words first. His wartime speeches , \"We shall fight on the beaches\" , turned national peril into national resilience , while film and radio carried the war effort into every home through the Blitz. Material mobilization matched the rhetoric: rationing and war-production measures redirected food, fuel, and factories to military needs.

The United States under Franklin Roosevelt became the \"arsenal of democracy.\" The Lend-Lease Act (1941) supplied Allied nations before America even entered the fighting; Fireside Chats built public support over the radio; war bonds and volunteer drives pulled citizens into the effort; and the War Production Board converted the civilian economy to wartime output, car factories building tanks almost overnight.

kt: The United States under Franklin Roosevelt

paragraphs.text: Note the common thread: both democracies mobilized totally in their demands on the economy, but did so by persuading a free public , with elections, a free press, and independent unions intact. Total mobilization did not require silencing the people.

callout.body: Connect back to Topic 7.3. The total-war methods of WWI, propaganda, rationing, economic mobilization, CONTINUE here, now amplified by radio and film. What is the change? Reach and intensity: mass media let governments speak directly into every living room, and the scale of production dwarfed 1914–1918. Use the continuity as evidence and name the change precisely.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: The Totalitarian States: Hitler and Stalin

paragraphs.text: Germany under Adolf Hitler mobilized through total control of information. The Ministry of Propaganda under Joseph Goebbels controlled all media , press, radio, film, and framed the war as national survival and expansion . Mobilization here was coercive: forced labor and conscription fed the war machine, and dissent was not permitted. This was the militarization of society at the cost of individual freedoms.

kt: militarization of society at the cost of individual freedoms.

paragraphs.text: The USSR under Joseph Stalin framed the conflict as the Great Patriotic War , a battle against fascism that summoned deep national feeling. Propaganda for unity rallied a population to staggering sacrifice, while political repression of dissent crushed any wavering. Collectivized agriculture and prioritized industrial production bent the entire command economy to military needs.

Here is the Key Concept's crucial second sentence in action: both states used ideologies, fascism and communism , to mobilize all of the state's resources, and, as totalitarian states , to repress basic freedoms and dominate many aspects of daily life . That is the line the democracies did not cross.

kt: repress basic freedoms and dominate many aspects of daily life

The difference is what mobilization was allowed to COST the population: in Germany and the USSR, ideology justified repressing basic freedoms and dominating daily life; in Britain and the U.S., mobilization ran through consent. Same toolkit, different limits, that single phrase answers the Learning Objective.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: New Technology, New Casualties

paragraphs.text: Total war reached new extremes through technology. The second Key Concept names them: new military technology and new tactics , including the atomic bomb , fire-bombing , and the waging of \"total war\" , led to increased levels of wartime casualties.

kt: new military technology and new tactics

paragraphs.text: Fire-bombing raids on cities like Dresden and Tokyo, and the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, put civilians squarely inside the target zone. The line between soldier and civilian, already blurred in WWI, collapsed , and entire cities became the battlefield. The result was casualty levels beyond even World War I.

kt: civilians squarely inside the target zone.

paragraphs.text: Now assemble the comparison the Learning Objective wants: all four powers mobilized propaganda, media, nationalism, and resources (the similarity), but only the totalitarian states repressed basic freedoms and dominated daily life (the difference), and new technology drove the whole war's human cost higher than ever. Carry the thread to Topic 7.8: when total state power over populations reaches its extreme , the result is mass atrocity , and into the 7.9 causation capstone.

Each war's technology made the next deadlier, and "total war" itself, erasing the soldier/civilian line, is a cause of rising casualties, not just a description. extraction.takeaway: World War II was a total war. Every great power used propaganda, art, media, and intensified nationalism to mobilize populations, both at home and in the colonies or former colonies , and turned its whole economy to the front. Two Western democracies mobilized through persuasion: Britain under Churchill (speeches, film, radio, rationing) and the United States under Roosevelt (Lend-Lease, Fireside Chats, war bonds, the War Production Board). Two totalitarian states mobilized through control: Germany under Hitler (Goebbels's Ministry of Propaganda, forced labor) and the USSR under Stalin (the Great Patriotic War, political repression), using fascism and communism to repress basic freedoms and dominate daily life. Same methods, different limits. And new technology, the atomic bomb and fire-bombing , plus the waging of total war put civilians in the target zone and drove wartime casualties beyond even World War I.

header.subtitle: Topic 7.8, Mass Atrocities After 1900 | AP World History: Modern

band.title: Extremism in Power
band.deck: When extremist groups seize unchecked state authority, the result can be the attempted destruction of entire populations. The Key Concept names the pattern: the rise of extremist groups in power led to genocide, ethnic violence, and atrocities across the twentieth century, from the Holocaust during World War II to the Armenian Genocide, the Holodomor, Cambodia, and Rwanda. This reading traces the causes and consequences that the CED identifies, and the structure that recurs across every case.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Hold the Key Concept's central claim: the rise of extremist groups in power led to the attempted destruction of specific populations. For each case, the Holocaust, the Armenian Genocide, the Holodomor, Cambodia, Rwanda, ask: what extremist ideology held power? What group was targeted? What conditions enabled it? What consequences followed?

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain how the rise of extremist groups led to the attempted destruction of specific populations, compare causes across at least two cases, and explain the consequences, cultural trauma, international legal frameworks like the Genocide Convention and the ICC, and political change.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: From Total War to Mass Atrocity

paragraphs.text: In Topic 7.7 you studied total war , governments mobilizing propaganda, media, nationalism, and their entire economies for conflict. You saw totalitarian states use ideology to repress basic freedoms and dominate daily life. Now follow that power to its most extreme result.

The Key Concept states the claim directly: the rise of extremist groups in power led to the attempted destruction of specific populations , notably the Nazi killing of the Jews in the Holocaust during World War II, and to other atrocities, acts of genocide, or ethnic violence. That is one sentence, read it carefully. It names a cause (extremism in power), a mechanism (attempted destruction), a specific example (the Holocaust), and a category (atrocities, genocide, ethnic violence).

kt: the rise of extremist groups in power led to the attempted destruction of specific populations

paragraphs.text: The Learning Objective asks you to explain the various causes and consequences of mass atrocities in the period from 1900 to the present. Notice the plural: causes (not just one) and consequences (not just the killing itself). The CED tests your ability to trace the causal chain from ideology to atrocity and from atrocity to aftermath.

kt: explain the various causes and consequences

paragraphs.text: Ground this in the thematic focus: Social Interactions and Organization (SIO) , how societies group their members and the norms that govern interactions between groups. Mass atrocities begin when a regime redefines who belongs to the society, and targets those it excludes.

For each case, trace the chain: extremist ideology → state power → dehumanization of a group → attempted destruction. That mechanism is what connects cause to consequence.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Extremism in Power: The Holocaust

paragraphs.text: The KC names the Holocaust directly: the Nazi killing of the Jews in the Holocaust during World War II. The Nazi regime's ideology of racial supremacy and antisemitism drove the systematic dehumanization of Jews through propaganda, legal exclusion, and escalating persecution.

The result was the systematic murder of approximately six million Jews , along with millions of Roma, disabled persons, political prisoners, and others. The Holocaust stands as the KC's central example of what happens when an extremist group holds unchecked state authority and defines a population as an enemy to be destroyed.

But the KC does not stop with the Holocaust, it says "and to other atrocities, acts of genocide, or ethnic violence." The CED's illustrative examples name four more cases. In each one, the same structure appears: an extremist ideology in power , the dehumanization of a defined group , crisis conditions that create opportunity, and unchecked state authority that removes restraints.

kt: "and to other atrocities, acts of genocide, or ethnic violence."

A strong comparison identifies what they share (the structure: extremist ideology + state power + dehumanization + crisis) and what differs (the specific ideology, the specific group targeted, the specific conditions). Comparing two cases sharpens the causal argument: if the same structure produces atrocity in different places and times, the structure itself is the cause.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Four Cases, One Pattern

paragraphs.text: Armenians in the Ottoman Empire during and after World War I. The Young Turk government launched a campaign of mass deportation and extermination , driven by fear of disloyalty during wartime and the desire to maintain territorial control. An estimated 1.5 million Armenians were killed. Connect to Topic 7.1 : the Ottoman Empire's decline and nationalist pressures created the crisis conditions.

kt: Armenians in the Ottoman Empire during and after World War I.

paragraphs.text: Ukraine in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s. The Holodomor was a man-made famine produced by forced collectivization and grain requisitioning under Stalin's regime, aimed at suppressing Ukrainian nationalism and consolidating state control. Millions perished. Connect to Topic 7.4 : the Five-Year Plans and collectivized agriculture were the mechanism the state weaponized.

kt: Ukraine in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s.

paragraphs.text: Cambodia during the late 1970s. The Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot attempted a radical agrarian communist transformation , emptying cities, abolishing institutions, targeting intellectuals, professionals, and ethnic minorities. An estimated 1.7 million people died through execution, forced labor, and starvation.

Tutsi in Rwanda in the 1990s. The Hutu majority government targeted the Tutsi population in a genocide that killed an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in roughly 100 days. Colonial policies had entrenched ethnic divisions by favoring the Tutsi minority; post-independence governments exploited rather than healed those divisions. The international community's failure to intervene allowed the killing to continue at extraordinary speed.

That recurring structure is the causal argument the CED tests. When you write about mass atrocities, name the specific ideology, the specific conditions, and the specific group, then explain how the structure produced the outcome.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Consequences — From Trauma to Law

paragraphs.text: Consequences reach beyond the killing itself. Cultural trauma carried by survivors and descendants shapes communities for generations, identities disrupted, histories interrupted, intergenerational pain that persists long after the violence ends.

International legal frameworks were built in direct response. The Genocide Convention (1948) , adopted after the Holocaust, defined genocide in international law for the first time. The International Criminal Court (ICC) was established to prosecute individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. These institutions exist because earlier atrocities revealed the absence of any legal framework to prevent or punish them.

Political change and reconciliation followed in specific cases: post-genocide Rwanda undertook community-based justice (gacaca courts) and national reconciliation; the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals established that individuals, not just states, bear criminal responsibility for atrocities.

But the repeated occurrence of genocide after the Convention's adoption, Cambodia in the 1970s, Rwanda in 1994, reveals a hard truth: naming and outlawing genocide did not prevent it. The gap between international law and international action is itself a consequence worth analyzing.

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 7.9, Causation in Global Conflict | AP World History: Modern

band.title: Weighing What Mattered Most
band.deck: Historians don't just list causes, they rank them. Topic 7.9 is the Unit 7 causation capstone, which means everything you studied in Topics 7.1 through 7.7 becomes evidence for a single analytical task: argue which causes of global conflict were most significant, and why. The skill is relative significance. The evidence is the whole unit. The argument is yours to build.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Keep two vocabulary terms in view: underlying causes , long-term structural factors that created conditions for conflict (imperial competition, nationalist movements, economic crisis), versus immediate triggers , specific events that set conflict in motion (the Sarajevo assassination, the German invasion of Poland). Both matter, but most historians argue underlying causes carry more analytical weight in a long-arc argument.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain the distinction between underlying causes and immediate triggers, identify at least three major causal categories from Unit 7, explain how causes braid together rather than operate independently, and build a defensible claim that ranks causes by relative significance using weighing language.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: The Capstone Question: Not What, But Which

paragraphs.text: You have spent the last seven topics answering the question what caused global conflict? The CED gave you the answer across thirteen Key Concepts: imperial competition, intense nationalism, a flawed alliance system, empire collapse, the Great Depression, fascist and totalitarian regimes, and new military technology. You can list them. Now comes the harder question: which causes mattered most?

This is the AP skill called relative significance , and it is what separates a descriptive list from a historical argument. Relative significance does not ask you to ignore some causes; it asks you to rank them and explain the ranking . Why did one cause do more work than another? What would have had to change for the conflict not to happen? What made some conditions necessary versus merely contributing?

kt: rank them and explain the ranking

paragraphs.text: The CED modeled this skill once, quietly, inside the WWII Key Concept. In Topic 7.6 you read: "the causes of World War II included the unsustainable peace settlement after World War I, the global economic crisis engendered by the Great Depression, continued imperialist aspirations, and especially the rise to power of fascist and totalitarian regimes." That word, especially , is a significance claim . It ranks one cause above the others. Your capstone task is to build your own, defend it with evidence, and use weighing language that makes the argument clear.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Causation
callout.body: The CED's "especially" is a model you can borrow, argue with, or beat. Notice what it does: it names the other causes, acknowledges them, and then ranks one above them. A weak answer lists all causes equally. A strong argument says "X was more significant than Y because..." and names a criterion, necessary condition, proximate cause, most explanatory power, widest impact. Name your criterion and defend it.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Underlying Causes vs. Immediate Triggers

paragraphs.text: The most important analytical move in a causation argument is sorting causes by type. Underlying causes are long-term structural factors that built pressure over years or decades, they created conditions in which conflict became possible, even likely. Immediate triggers are specific events that set conflict in motion, they lit the fuse, but they did not make the powder keg.

For World War I: the underlying causes were imperial competition and rivalry, intense nationalism across Europe, the hair-trigger alliance system (Triple Alliance vs. Triple Entente), and the territorial decline of older empires. These were all in place by 1914. The immediate trigger was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand on June 28, 1914, one gunshot, fired by a nineteen-year-old who had already failed once that morning and thought he had failed again.

For World War II: the underlying causes were the unsustainable peace settlement at Versailles, the Great Depression, and continued imperialist competition. The more proximate cause , the one the CED marks with "especially", was the rise of fascist and totalitarian regimes: Nazi Germany under Hitler, which actively converted those underlying conditions into aggressive militarism, rearmament, and territorial expansion. Germany's invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939 was the trigger, but the regime was the mechanism that made invasion possible.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Argumentation
callout.body: Ask yourself: if you removed this cause, would the conflict still have happened? The alliance system in 1914 was so rigid that a local Austro-Serbian conflict dragged in six great powers in five weeks, remove the alliance system and the assassination stays local. Remove the assassination and the war probably still happens, just from a different spark. That test, "would the conflict happen without this cause?", is one way to rank relative significance.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Braided Causes: When Factors Work Together

paragraphs.text: The most common mistake in a causation argument is treating causes as if they operated independently, one after another. In history, causes braid , they reinforce each other, enable each other, and interact in ways that make the whole more explosive than any single strand.

Consider the WWII causal chain. The unsustainable peace at Versailles (Topic 7.5) imposed reparations and humiliation on Germany, creating economic crisis and political resentment. The Great Depression (Topic 7.4) then deepened that economic crisis, discrediting democratic governments and making radical political movements suddenly credible to millions of desperate, angry voters. Into that environment rose the Nazi regime (Topic 7.6), which transformed economic desperation and nationalist resentment into organized, militarized aggression. The regime then pursued imperialist expansion in the name of German destiny, seizing the Rhineland, Austria, the Sudetenland, and finally Poland.

This is not four separate causes, it is one braid : Versailles → Depression → fascist regime → aggressive militarism → war. A strong significance argument doesn't just identify the braid; it argues which strand carried the most weight. Was it the conditions (Versailles, the Depression) that made everything else possible? Or the regime that converted conditions into action? That question, which strand mattered most, is exactly what relative significance asks.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Causation
callout.body: Distinguish contributing factors from necessary conditions. A contributing factor made conflict more likely but was not indispensable. A necessary condition was one without which the conflict would not have occurred, or would have been fundamentally different. Necessary conditions carry more argumentative weight than contributing factors. If you can identify a necessary condition in the causal chain, argue for it, that is your significance claim.

sections.label: Key Concept
sections.heading: Building the Argument: Weighing Language

paragraphs.text: A significance argument requires precision language , terms that signal you are ranking, not just listing. The AP exam rewards students who use weighing language explicitly, because it shows the reader that you understand you are making a judgment, not just describing events.

Here are the moves available to you. "Most significant because" , names your top-ranked cause and your criterion for ranking it. "More significant than" , makes an explicit comparison between two causes, which is stronger than ranking in isolation. "Necessary condition" , identifies a cause without which the conflict could not have occurred in the form it took. "Underlying cause" versus "immediate trigger" , sorts causes by proximity to the event. "Enabled by" , traces how one cause made another cause possible.

What to avoid: "equally important" , that is not a ranking. "All the causes combined" , that is not a significance claim. "There are many causes" , that is a description, not an argument. You are allowed to disagree with the CED's "especially", but you have to disagree with specific evidence, not just a different list. A historian who argues against the consensus has to argue harder, not differently.

callout.body: Write the claim before you write the evidence. Without [Cause X], [Cause Y] and [Cause Z] would not have produced the same outcome." Then fill in the evidence. A claim that strong is worth defending with three topics of specific evidence from Unit 7.

extraction.topicLabel: 8.1 - Setting the Stage for the Cold War and Decolonization

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 8.1, Setting the Stage for the Cold War and Decolonization | AP World History: Modern

band.title: Setting the Stage
band.deck: How unfulfilled promises after World War I, the economic ruin of European empires after World War II, and the rise of two rival superpowers created the conditions for both decolonization and the Cold War after 1945.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Track two things as you read: (1) a promise that was made but not kept after WWI, and (2) one way that WWII changed who held power in the world. Strong historians notice both the gap between rhetoric and reality and the material conditions that shift power.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to explain how unfulfilled post-WWI promises, WWII's economic cost for European empires, and the rise of the U.S. and Soviet Union together created the conditions for decolonization and Cold War rivalry after 1945.

sections.label: Contextualization
sections.heading: The Promise That Wasn't Kept: Self-Determination After WWI

paragraphs.text: When World War I ended in 1918, U.S. President Woodrow Wilson announced his Fourteen Points , a framework for a just peace. Point Fourteen created the League of Nations. But scattered through Wilson's plan was an idea that electrified people from Egypt to India to West Africa: self-determination . Peoples, Wilson suggested, should have the right to choose their own form of government. For colonized peoples who had supplied armies, labor, and resources to European powers throughout the war, this was more than an abstract principle. It felt like a promise.

The Paris Peace Conference of 1919 delivered something different. The Allied powers, Britain, France, Italy, Japan, and the United States, divided Germany's former colonies and the territories of the collapsed Ottoman Empire among themselves through the League of Nations Mandate System . Britain gained control over Palestine, Iraq, and Tanganyika. France took Syria, Lebanon, and parts of West Africa. The Mandate System gave European powers formal authority over millions of people in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East, using the language of "trusteeship" and "civilizing mission" to dress up what was, in practice, an expansion of colonial control.

Between the wars, nationalist movements organized across the colonized world. The Indian National Congress , led by figures including Mohandas Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru , built a mass independence movement rooted in civil disobedience and noncooperation with British rule. Pan-African activists organized congresses demanding recognition of African peoples' political rights. Vietnamese nationalists agitated against French rule. In each case, European colonial governments responded with a combination of token concessions and repression. The movements were weakened, co-opted, or suppressed, but not destroyed.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Contextualization
callout.body: Before you can explain the Cold War or decolonization, you need to understand why 1945 felt so charged to people living in colonized countries. The gap between Wilson's self-determination rhetoric and the Mandate System's reality left a reservoir of grievance that World War II would turn into action. Contextualization for Topic 8.1 means tracing that connection: the interwar period is part of the context that made the post-1945 world.

sections.label: Key Concept, KC-6.2.II
sections.heading: Empires Come Home to Collect: WWII and the Cost of Empire

paragraphs.text: World War II did not just kill soldiers. It exhausted economies. Britain entered the war as the center of the world's largest empire. It emerged in 1945 with debts it could not repay, a treasury that was nearly empty, and a military stretched across dozens of territories it could no longer afford to police. The United States had terminated Lend-Lease aid to Britain in September 1945, weeks after the war ended, forcing Britain to negotiate a painful American loan whose terms required dismantling imperial trade preferences. The empire's fiscal foundation was gone.

In this context, independence movements that had been suppressed for decades suddenly faced a weakened adversary. India was the first and most dramatic case. The Indian National Congress , strengthened by decades of organizing, combined mass civil disobedience with political negotiations that the exhausted British government could not resist. In 1947, Britain announced it would transfer power, and Nehru became the first Prime Minister of an independent India. The partition of British India into India and Pakistan accompanied independence, producing one of the largest and most devastating mass migrations in human history.

Ghana followed a decade later, in 1957. Kwame Nkrumah , a pan-Africanist who had studied in the United States and Britain, organized a mass independence movement in the Gold Coast that Britain could not suppress without the resources it no longer had. Ghana's independence under Nkrumah was the first moment of decolonization in sub-Saharan Africa, and it sent a signal across the continent. By the early 1960s, dozens of African nations would follow.

The pattern was consistent: WWII had weakened European colonial powers, and independence movements that had been building for decades were now strong enough to succeed. The dissolution of empires and the restructuring of states across Asia and Africa, which the CED calls the result of increasing anti-imperialist sentiment, was the direct consequence of two intersecting forces: grievances that predated 1939, and a colonial system too exhausted after 1945 to hold on.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Causation
callout.body: Strong causation analysis identifies both immediate and underlying causes. The immediate cause of Indian independence in 1947 was British exhaustion after WWII. The underlying cause was decades of organizing by the Indian National Congress against a colonial system that had broken its own promise of self-determination. Both matter. AP questions on decolonization reward analysis that connects the short-term trigger (imperial exhaustion) to the long-term cause (anti-imperialist sentiment built since WWI).

sections.label: Key Concept, KC-6.2.IV.C.i
sections.heading: Two Powers Standing: The Superpower Rivalry Emerges

paragraphs.text: While European empires were exhausting themselves, the United States and the Soviet Union were growing stronger. The United States entered WWII as a powerful industrial economy and emerged from it transformed. American GDP nearly doubled during the war years as factories shifted from consumer goods to weapons, aircraft, and ships. By 1945, the United States held roughly half of the world's industrial output, controlled significant nuclear technology, and had military forces positioned across Europe, the Pacific, and beyond. The war had done to the U.S. economy what it had done to Britain's and France's economies in reverse: it made it stronger.

The Soviet Union paid a catastrophic human cost, an estimated 27 million deaths, but it also emerged transformed. Wartime industrialization had dramatically expanded Soviet industrial capacity, particularly in the Ural mountains and Siberia, far from German advance. The Red Army that defeated Nazi Germany was the largest land force in the world, and Soviet scientists would develop nuclear weapons by 1949. The Soviet Union emerged as the world's other superpower, holding an ideology, Marxism-Leninism , that promised liberation to colonized and exploited peoples everywhere, making it an attractive alternative to the Western capitalist order for nationalist movements in Asia and Africa.

The two powers had fundamentally different visions for the post-war world, and those visions immediately collided. The United States launched the Marshall Plan in 1948, committing $13 billion in economic aid to rebuild Western Europe, and to anchor it within the American sphere of influence. The Soviet Union extended its control over Eastern Europe through communist governments installed in Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany. These two blocs, one centered on Washington, one on Moscow, formalized into NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955), military alliances that divided Europe and much of the world into rival camps.

The Cold War that resulted was not a single event. It was a structural condition, a state of continuous competition, ideological rivalry, proxy conflict, and arms buildup, that shaped global politics for the next four decades. Understanding it requires understanding where it came from: the technological and economic gains of the victorious nations after WWII had fundamentally shifted the global balance of power, creating two superpowers with rival ideologies and the capacity to act on them globally.

The Soviet Union extended its control over Eastern Europe through communist governments installed in Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany. These two blocs, one centered on Washington, one on Moscow, formalized into NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955), military alliances that divided Europe and much of the world into rival camps.

The Cold War that resulted was not a single event. It was a structural condition, a state of continuous competition, ideological rivalry, proxy conflict, and arms buildup, that shaped global politics for the next four decades. Understanding it requires understanding where it came from: the technological and economic gains of the victorious nations after WWII had fundamentally shifted the global balance of power, creating two superpowers with rival ideologies and the capacity to act on them globally.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Contextualization
callout.body: The Cold War did not begin in 1947 or 1949. It had roots that reached back through WWII, the interwar period, and beyond. Explaining the historical context of the Cold War after 1945 means connecting at least two broader developments: the shift in the balance of power that WWII produced, and the unresolved tensions from the failure of post-WWI self-determination. Both sets of conditions mattered. The Cold War emerged in a world shaped by both.

extraction.takeaway: Three forces set the stage for the post-1945 world: (1) unfulfilled promises of self-determination after WWI created lasting anti-imperialist sentiment; (2) WWII exhausted Britain and France, weakening their ability to maintain colonial empires and accelerating decolonization; (3) WWII's technological and economic gains produced two rival superpowers, the U.S. and the Soviet Union, whose competition for global influence defined the Cold War. Decolonization and the Cold War were not separate stories. They happened simultaneously, shaped each other, and both grew from the same post-WWII moment.

sections.label: Causation, KC-6.2.IV.C.ii
sections.heading: Two Worldviews Collide: The Ideological Roots of the Cold War

paragraphs.text: World War II ended with two powers standing where five had stood before. The United States and the Soviet Union had both been strengthened by the war, and both had watched Europe's old empires exhaust themselves. But the two surviving superpowers held fundamentally incompatible visions for the world they now dominated.

The United States promoted liberal capitalism : open markets, multiparty democracy, free elections, and individual rights. American leaders believed that economic freedom and political freedom were inseparable, and that both were best protected by a U.S.-led international order. By 1945, the United States held roughly half the world's industrial output, controlled nuclear technology, and had military forces positioned across Europe, the Pacific, and beyond. It had the power to build the world it wanted.

The Soviet Union promoted Marxism-Leninism : state control of the economy, collective ownership, one-party communist rule, and the historical argument that capitalism was a system of exploitation that would inevitably be replaced by communism. Soviet leaders believed they were leading the vanguard of global liberation, and that every country that turned communist was a victory for human progress. The USSR had suffered 27 million deaths in WWII but had industrialized rapidly and emerged with the world's largest land army. By 1949, it had nuclear weapons too.

The two powers moved immediately to expand their spheres of influence. The United States announced the Truman Doctrine in 1947, committing to support any government resisting communist takeover, and backed it with $400 million for Greece and Turkey. The Marshall Plan (1948) committed $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe, explicitly to prevent communist parties from winning power in economically devastated democracies. The Soviet Union, meanwhile, consolidated control over Eastern Europe, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany, installing communist governments backed by the Red Army behind what Winston Churchill called the Iron Curtain .

callout.label: AP Thinking, Causation
callout.body: The Cold War did not happen because the U.S. and USSR disliked each other. It happened because WWII fundamentally shifted the global balance of power, leaving two rival superpowers with incompatible ideologies and the capacity to act on them globally. The cause of the Cold War was structural: the same war that destroyed European empires elevated two powers that could not coexist peacefully because they held fundamentally different beliefs about how societies should be organized.

sections.label: Causation, Effects on International Relations
sections.heading: A Divided World: Alliances, Arms Race, and Proxy Wars

paragraphs.text: The ideological struggle between capitalism and communism did not stay in the realm of rhetoric. It reshaped the physical and military architecture of the post-war world. In 1949, the United States and eleven Western democracies formed the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) , a formal military alliance committing each member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. When West Germany joined in 1955, the Soviet Union responded with the Warsaw Pact , a Soviet-led military alliance that brought the Eastern European satellite states under unified military command. The Cold War divide was now institutionalized.

The ideological struggle also became existential with the nuclear arms race . The United States had used atomic bombs in 1945. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949, years earlier than U.S. intelligence had predicted. Within a decade, both sides had developed hydrogen bombs hundreds of times more powerful. By the late 1950s, both possessed enough warheads to destroy civilization. This produced the doctrine of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) : both sides understood that a nuclear first strike would trigger a response that would annihilate both. The Cold War stayed cold, but only barely.

The conflict turned violent through proxy conflicts , wars where the United States and Soviet Union backed opposing sides without directly fighting each other. The Korean War (1950–1953) began when Soviet-backed North Korea invaded U.S.-backed South Korea. Three years of brutal fighting killed over 3 million people, most of them Korean civilians. When the armistice was signed in 1953, the Korean peninsula was divided at almost exactly the same line where it had started, the 38th parallel. Nothing had changed on the map. Everything had changed in human cost.

The Vietnam War (1955–1975) followed a similar logic. Communist North Vietnam, supported by the Soviet Union and China, fought to unite the country under communist rule. South Vietnam, supported by the United States, resisted. Over two decades of escalating conflict killed over 2 million Vietnamese civilians and left the country devastated. The United States withdrew its forces in 1973. North Vietnam reunified the country under communist rule in 1975. The world's most powerful military could not win a proxy war fought in a poor country by a determined opponent who was willing to accept far greater losses.

sections.label: Argumentation, KC-6.2.V.B
sections.heading: A Third Way: The Non-Aligned Movement

paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepted the Cold War's binary. In April 1955, representatives of 29 Asian and African nations gathered in Bandung, Indonesia, for a conference that had no superpower host and no superpower agenda. They came from countries that had recently won independence from European empires, or were still fighting for it. Their shared experience was not of capitalism versus communism. It was of colonialism: the experience of being governed, exploited, and dismissed by foreign powers for generations.

Sukarno of Indonesia, who convened the conference, argued that the Cold War was a problem created by the old world order, and that newly independent nations had no obligation to inherit it. His opening address at Bandung invoked the idea that the nations gathered there represented the majority of humanity, and that they had the right to define their own future. Non-alignment was not neutrality, it was an assertion of sovereignty. The Bandung Conference produced a statement of ten principles including respect for national sovereignty, non-aggression, and non-interference in other nations' internal affairs.

Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana, who had argued for African independence for decades and would lead the Gold Coast to become the first sub-Saharan African state to gain independence in 1957, framed the issue in terms of economic dependency. Accepting U.S. or Soviet development aid meant accepting political conditions that would reproduce the dependency of colonial rule. True independence required economic independence from both superpowers, not merely the replacement of one foreign master with another.

India's Jawaharlal Nehru , one of the architects of what became the Non-Aligned Movement, argued that the Cold War bloc system reproduced the imperial pattern: great powers treating smaller nations as pieces in their own game. Non-alignment was an active ideology, a belief about how the world should work, rooted in the conviction that newly independent nations had both the right and the responsibility to chart their own course. The Non-Aligned Movement was, in the terms of the AP CED, groups and individuals promoting alternatives to the existing economic, political, and social orders.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Argumentation
callout.body: An AP argumentation claim about the Non-Aligned Movement needs to do more than describe it. It needs to explain what the Non-Aligned Movement reveals about the Cold War era, and connect it to broader patterns. The strongest argument treats the Non-Aligned Movement as evidence that the Cold War's binary framing was always contested: newly independent nations did not simply choose between capitalism and communism; many explicitly rejected both as forms of foreign domination. Sukarno and Nkrumah are not just names to drop, they are evidence of a broader historical pattern.

extraction.takeaway: The Cold War emerged from WWII's fundamental shift in the global balance of power: two rival superpowers, with incompatible ideologies, competed for global influence. The effects reshaped international relations, NATO and the Warsaw Pact institutionalized the divide, the nuclear arms race made the conflict existential, and proxy wars in Korea and Vietnam made it violent. But the Cold War's binary was always contested: the Non-Aligned Movement, launched at the 1955 Bandung Conference by leaders including Sukarno and Nkrumah, asserted that newly independent nations had the right to define their own beliefs about the world order, not simply choose between two versions of superpower control.

sections.label: Comparison, KC-6.2.IV.D
sections.heading: Blocs and Treaties: Alliances as Instruments of Influence

paragraphs.text: The most visible early effects of the Cold War were institutional: two new military alliances that divided Europe and extended superpower reach across the globe. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) , formed in 1949, committed twelve Western democracies to collective defense under American leadership. An attack on any member would be treated as an attack on all. U.S. nuclear weapons, military bases, and forces stationed across Western Europe made NATO the primary instrument through which the United States projected power and maintained influence over its allies.

NATO was not purely defensive. Joining meant accepting U.S. military presence on your soil, aligning your foreign policy with Washington, and hosting American nuclear weapons. Smaller member states gained security guarantees, but surrendered a degree of sovereignty. The alliance extended U.S. influence through multilateral commitment, binding Western Europe to American leadership through treaty obligation rather than direct occupation.

The Warsaw Pact (1955) formalized the Soviet bloc's military arrangement. Eight Eastern European states committed to mutual defense under Soviet command, but the Warsaw Pact served a different function than NATO. Soviet troops were already stationed throughout Eastern Europe, installing and sustaining communist governments. The Pact gave legal form to what was already military reality. The Brezhnev Doctrine , articulated in 1968 after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia, made the difference explicit: the USSR claimed the right to intervene militarily in any socialist state where socialism was threatened, regardless of that state's preferences. The Warsaw Pact was not a multilateral alliance, it was an instrument of Soviet hegemonic control.

callout.label: AP Thinking, Comparison
callout.body: NATO and the Warsaw Pact look symmetrical, two rival military alliances. But comparison reveals an important difference in how each served its superpower. NATO extended U.S. influence through multilateral treaty commitments with nominal equality among members. The Warsaw Pact enforced Soviet hegemony through direct military presence and the explicit right of intervention, a fundamentally different relationship between the dominant power and its partners.

sections.label: Causation, KC-6.2.IV.D
sections.heading: The Balance of Terror: Nuclear Proliferation and Deterrence

paragraphs.text: The most consequential effect of the Cold War ideological struggle was the nuclear arms race . The United States had held a monopoly on atomic weapons from 1945 to 1949. When the Soviet Union tested its first nuclear device in August 1949, years ahead of American predictions, it instantly transformed the strategic situation. Neither superpower could now destroy the other without risking its own annihilation.

Both sides then developed thermonuclear weapons , hydrogen bombs hundreds of times more powerful than the atomic bombs used in 1945. By the late 1950s, both possessed enough warheads to destroy civilization many times over. Nuclear proliferation spread beyond the two superpowers: Britain tested a nuclear weapon in 1952, France in 1960, and China in 1964. Each new nuclear power extended the arms race and complicated the strategic picture.

The doctrine of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) defined the Cold War's peculiar logic: if either superpower launched a first strike, the other would retain enough surviving weapons to retaliate and annihilate the attacker. Both sides knew that nuclear war meant the destruction of both. This paradox deterred direct military confrontation between the superpowers, but it did not end competition. It redirected it. Nuclear deterrence made a third world war between the great powers virtually unthinkable, but it simultaneously made proxy wars, fought by other people, in other countries, the dominant method of superpower competition.

callout.body: The nuclear arms race produced a paradox: weapons so destructive that using them was irrational, which meant competition had to flow through other channels. MAD caused proxy wars. Nuclear deterrence constrained direct superpower conflict so effectively that the Korean Peninsula, Angola, and Nicaragua became the actual battlefields of Cold War competition. Understanding this causal chain is essential for AP comparison arguments about why both superpowers chose proxy methods.

sections.label: Comparison, KC-6.2.IV.D
sections.heading: Wars by Other Hands: Proxy Conflicts in Three Regions

paragraphs.text: Proxy wars became the Cold War's dominant form of violence: conflicts where the United States and Soviet Union backed opposing sides without directly fighting each other, extending their competition into postcolonial states in Latin America, Africa, and Asia. Each proxy war followed a similar structural pattern, local forces, superpower arms and funding, ideological framing, while revealing important differences in how each superpower operated.

The Korean War (1950–1953) was the first major test. Soviet-backed North Korea invaded U.S.-backed South Korea in June 1950. The United States led a UN coalition to defend the South; China entered when American forces approached its border. Three years of grinding combat killed over 3 million people, most of them Korean civilians. The armistice in 1953 restored the pre-war division at the 38th parallel. Korea established the proxy-war pattern: superpower clients doing the fighting, superpower interests defining the stakes, the local population absorbing the cost.

The Angolan Civil War (1975–2002) demonstrated how proxy competition moved to Africa as decolonization created new states and new openings. When Portugal withdrew from Angola in 1975, three liberation movements contested power. The USSR and Cuba backed the MPLA (Movimento Popular de Libertação de Angola), a Marxist movement that controlled the capital Luanda. The United States and apartheid South Africa backed UNITA and the FNLA, anti-communist factions fighting from the interior and south. Cuban combat troops, not just advisors, deployed alongside MPLA forces. The war lasted 27 years and killed hundreds of thousands of Angolans. Both superpowers framed their involvement in ideological terms: the USSR as socialist solidarity and anti-imperialist support; the United States as containment of communist expansion in Africa.

The Sandinista–Contras conflict in Nicaragua brought proxy war to Latin America. In 1979, the Sandinista movement overthrew the U.S.-backed Somoza dictatorship. The Reagan administration, alarmed by a Soviet-aligned government in Central America, funded and organized the Contras, a counterrevolutionary insurgency, to destabilize the Sandinista government. The Soviet Union and Cuba supplied the Sandinistas with arms and advisors. The U.S. Congress eventually restricted Contra funding, leading to the Iran-Contra scandal (1986–1987) when the Reagan administration secretly diverted funds from arms sales to Iran to continue financing the Contras, revealing the depth of U.S. commitment to proxy methods even when legally prohibited.

Comparing these methods, not just cataloguing them, is what AP LO C requires.

band.title: Spread of Communism After 1900
band.deck: How internal tension and Japanese aggression produced communist revolution in China, how the Great Leap Forward turned state economic control into catastrophe, and how redistribution movements in Vietnam, Ethiopia, India, and Iran took strikingly different paths to the same goal.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: This topic has two distinct learning objectives: LO D covers China (causes and consequences of communist seizure of power) and LO E covers redistribution movements across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. Track both as you read. For China, trace the two causes the CED specifies: internal tension AND Japanese aggression. For the redistribution cases, note what drove each movement and what effect it produced.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to: (1) explain the two causes of China's communist revolution and the consequences of the Great Leap Forward; and (2) explain the causes and effects of at least two of the four CED redistribution examples, Vietnam, Ethiopia, Kerala/India, and Iran.

sections.label: Causation, KC-6.2.I.i / LO D
sections.heading: How China Turned Communist: Two Causes

paragraphs.text: The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) was founded in 1921, in a country still reeling from the collapse of the Qing dynasty (1912). Without a stable imperial government, warlords controlled regional territories; the Kuomintang (KMT) , China's Nationalist Party, struggled to unify the country under Chiang Kai-shek. Peasants made up the vast majority of the Chinese population, and most lived as tenant farmers under landlords who controlled the land. The promise of land redistribution made the CCP's message compelling in the countryside.

The first cause of communist revolution was internal tension : political fragmentation, warlordism, the KMT's failure to build stable governance, and the deep inequality between landlords and a landless peasantry created the conditions for revolutionary organizing. But internal tension alone had not produced a communist victory in the 1920s or 1930s, the KMT still held the major cities and most of the military strength.

The second cause was Japanese aggression . Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and launched a full-scale invasion of China in 1937. The KMT bore primary responsibility for resisting Japan in direct military confrontation, and suffered catastrophic losses in men, equipment, and political legitimacy. Meanwhile, the CCP operated from the rural countryside and the communist stronghold at Yan'an, building popular networks, promising land reform to peasants, and framing itself as the authentic resistance movement. The Long March (1934–1935) , the CCP's grueling 6,000-mile retreat from KMT encirclement, became the founding myth of Chinese communism, and Mao Zedong consolidated leadership during it.

After Japan's defeat in 1945, civil war between the KMT and CCP resumed immediately. The KMT, exhausted, corrupt, and having lost mass popular support, collapsed rapidly. On October 1, 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China from Tiananmen Gate. The KMT retreated to Taiwan. The world's most populous country had become communist.

kt: On October 1, 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China

callout.label: AP Thinking, Causation
callout.body: The CED identifies two causes of China's communist revolution: internal tension (political fragmentation, warlordism, KMT failure, peasant land hunger) and Japanese aggression (which devastated the KMT while the CCP built rural support networks). AP causation requires naming both causes and explaining how each contributed, not just listing one. Both were necessary; neither alone was sufficient.

sections.label: Causation, KC-6.3.I.A.ii / LO D
sections.heading: The Great Leap Forward: State Control and Its Consequences

paragraphs.text: The Great Leap Forward (1958–1962) was Mao's attempt to transform China from an agrarian society into a socialist industrial power within a single generation, through the state's total control of the national economy. It represents the CED key concept directly: communist government control of the national economy, repressive policies, and negative repercussions for the population.

Collectivization reorganized China's villages into massive people's communes , state-directed collective units that replaced family farming. Communes were assigned production quotas for both grain and steel. The signature policy was the backyard steel furnace campaign : every commune was required to produce steel using small clay kilns. Families melted down metal tools, cooking pots, and door hinges to meet the quota. The steel produced was brittle and largely unusable. Meanwhile, the loss of farm tools contributed directly to the agricultural collapse that followed.

The mechanism of catastrophe was production reporting . Local officials competed to report record harvests, inflating figures by factors of two, three, or more, to demonstrate loyalty and avoid being labeled "rightists." After Defense Minister Peng Dehuai was purged in 1959 for privately criticizing the Leap, no official dared report honest numbers. The state then extracted grain based on the inflated reports, leaving villages without food, without even seed grain for the next planting.

The result was the Great Chinese Famine (1959–1961) , an estimated 15–55 million deaths, the deadliest famine in recorded history. The famine was not caused by drought. It was caused by state economic control: production quotas, collectivization, inflated reporting, and forced grain procurement all operating simultaneously. This is the CED's "negative repercussions for the population" operating at catastrophic scale.

sections.label: Causation / Comparison, KC-6.2.II.D.i / LO E
sections.heading: Four Paths to Redistribution: Vietnam, Ethiopia, India, and Iran

paragraphs.text: While China was the most dramatic case, the drive to redistribute land and resources shaped politics across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. The CED identifies four illustrative examples, and what makes them valuable for AP work is the range of paths they represent.

Communist Revolution for Vietnamese independence: Ho Chi Minh 's Viet Minh combined anti-colonial nationalism with communist ideology, mobilizing Vietnamese peasants with promises of land redistribution from landlords to the rural poor. The First Indochina War (1946–1954) against France ended with the defeat of French forces at Dien Bien Phu and the division of Vietnam at the 17th parallel. Cause: colonial occupation + rural land inequality. Effect: independence, partition, land redistribution to peasants, and a divided Vietnam that became a Cold War battleground.

Mengistu Haile Mariam in Ethiopia: The Derg , a Marxist military junta, overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974, then nationalized land, industries, and businesses under Mengistu. Land reform broke up large aristocratic and religious estates. But the government's Red Terror (1977–1978), a brutal suppression of political opponents, killed tens of thousands, and civil war combined with collectivization produced famine. Cause: imperial inequality + military coup. Effect: redistribution alongside brutal political repression and civil war.

Land reform in Kerala and other states within India: The Communist Party of India won state elections in Kerala in 1957, the first democratically elected communist government in the world, and passed sweeping land reform legislation, redistributing holdings from landlords to tenant farmers. Other Indian states followed with similar reforms in the 1950s–1970s. Cause: extreme landlord-tenant inequality + communist electoral organizing. Effect: significant redistribution without revolution or civil war, improving conditions for tenant farmers and landless laborers through democratic legislative means.

strong: Land reform in Kerala and other states within India:

paragraphs.text: White Revolution in Iran: Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi launched the White Revolution in 1963, a top-down modernization and land redistribution program designed partly to preempt communist rural organizing and satisfy American pressure for reform. The Shah redistributed land from large religious and aristocratic landholdings to rural peasants, disrupting traditional power structures. Cause: fear of communist organizing + U.S. pressure for modernization. Effect: redistribution that displaced traditional elites and accelerated urbanization, contributing to the social tensions that produced the Iranian Revolution of 1979 .

header.name: First & 10 Reading
header.subtitle: Topic 8.5, Decolonization After 1900 | AP World History: Modern

band.title: Decolonization After 1900
band.deck: How nationalist leaders built mass movements, why some colonies negotiated independence while others fought for it, and how the boundaries drawn by colonial empires became the fault lines of new conflicts after independence.

support.heading: Before You Read
support.body: Track three threads as you read: (1) the strategies nationalist leaders used, what made them effective in their specific colonial context; (2) what conditions pushed a colony toward negotiated independence vs. armed struggle; (3) how inherited colonial boundaries produced conflicts that outlasted colonial rule. AP LO F asks you to compare these processes, so focus on what made paths similar and different, not just on memorizing case names.

support.heading: Reading Target
support.body: By the end, you should be able to: explain the strategy of at least two CED nationalist leaders/parties; compare at least one negotiated-independence case with one armed-struggle case, explaining one factor that accounts for the difference; and explain how at least one regional, religious, or ethnic movement challenged inherited imperial boundaries.

sections.label: Causation, KC-6.2.II.A
sections.heading: The Leaders and the Parties: Four Paths to the Same Demand

paragraphs.text: Independence movements across Asia and Africa were not spontaneous, they were built by organizations, parties, and leaders who mobilized populations and developed strategies for challenging colonial power. The CED identifies four illustrative leaders and parties, each representing a distinct approach to seeking autonomy or independence from imperial rule.

The Indian National Congress (INC) , founded in 1885, built India's independence movement over six decades. Under Mohandas Gandhi , the INC developed satyagraha , nonviolent civil disobedience, as its core strategy. The Salt March of 1930, in which Gandhi led thousands in a 240-mile walk to collect salt illegally, was a mass act of defiance against British tax law that drew global attention and made British repression politically costly at home. The INC also built cross-caste coalitions and mobilized rural India in ways that earlier elite-dominated nationalist organizations had not. Jawaharlal Nehru , Gandhi's political partner and successor, directed the INC's international diplomacy and would become India's first Prime Minister after the Indian Independence Act of 1947.

Ho Chi Minh founded the Viet Minh in 1941, combining Vietnamese nationalism with communist ideology. On September 2, 1945, pointedly choosing the same day Japan formally surrendered, he declared Vietnamese independence, quoting the American Declaration of Independence and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man. France refused to accept the declaration and fought the First Indochina War (1946–1954). The Viet Minh's defeat of France at Dien Bien Phu (1954) forced French withdrawal. Ho Chi Minh's strategy combined mass rural organization, armed resistance, and international political framing, demonstrating that the colonial power's refusal to negotiate forces an armed path.

Kwame Nkrumah returned to the Gold Coast in 1947 after a decade studying in the United States and attending the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester. He split from the conservative UGCC to found the Convention People's Party (CPP) with the slogan "Self-Government Now." Nkrumah's strategy was mass mobilization: the CPP organized workers, market women, youth, and veterans, constituencies the UGCC's elite leadership had ignored. His Positive Action campaign (January 1950) launched nonviolent strikes and boycotts; he was arrested and imprisoned. But the CPP won the 1951 elections while Nkrumah was in prison, and the British released him to govern. Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African nation to achieve independence in 1957 , and Nkrumah became the symbol of African decolonization globally.

kt: Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African nation to achieve independence in 1957

paragraphs.text: Gamal Abdel Nasser led a military coup in Egypt in 1952, overthrowing the British-backed monarchy. Egypt had been nominally independent since 1922 but remained economically controlled by Britain and France through the Suez Canal Company. Nasser's nationalization of the Suez Canal in 1956 transformed the question of sovereignty from political to economic, he was asserting that Egypt would control its own resources. Britain and France responded with military force, but the United States and Soviet Union both pressured them to withdraw, revealing that European imperial power in the postwar world was constrained by Cold War superpower politics.
